entry.title: Active and Volumetric Stereo
entry.content:
Beyond Passive Vision: Active Stereo and Volumetric 3D Reconstruction

How computers use structured light, shadows, and volumetric reasoning to reconstruct the shape of objects — without solving the correspondence problem.

Introduction: The Hardest Part of Stereo Vision

Imagine you are given two photographs of the same coffee mug, taken from slightly different positions. Your task is to figure out the 3D shape of the mug. Conceptually, the approach is clear: find matching points across the two images, then use triangulation to recover each point’s position in 3D space. Easy enough in theory.

But in practice, this task — called the correspondence problem — is notoriously difficult. How do you know whether pixel $(100, 200)$ in the left image actually corresponds to pixel $(98, 197)$ in the right image? On a uniformly white ceramic mug, most pixels look nearly identical. A small patch of the surface could match dozens of other patches. Texture-less regions, reflective surfaces, and repeated patterns all make the correspondence problem ambiguous, and errors in correspondence translate directly into errors in 3D reconstruction.


The methods covered in previous discussions — triangulation, structure from motion, bundle adjustment — all assumed that the correspondence problem had already been solved. But as we push toward practical 3D reconstruction systems, this assumption becomes the main bottleneck.

This article explores two families of techniques that take radically different approaches to circumventing or sidestepping the correspondence problem entirely. Active stereo sidesteps it by projecting known patterns into the scene, making correspondences trivially identifiable. Volumetric stereo inverts the problem altogether, asking not “which pixels correspond?” but rather “which candidate 3D points are geometrically consistent with the images?”

Both approaches have powered real-world applications — from the sub-millimeter digitization of Renaissance masterpieces to the depth sensors embedded in consumer gaming devices — and together they represent a rich toolkit for shape acquisition that complements the passive methods we have discussed so far.

Part 1: Active Stereo — Illuminating the Correspondence Problem Away

The Core Idea

The fundamental insight of active stereo is elegantly simple: if you do not know which parts of the scene correspond across your two cameras, just mark them yourself. Instead of passively relying on the scene’s existing texture, you project a known pattern onto the object and let the pattern carry the correspondence information.

In a standard stereo setup, you have two cameras. Active stereo replaces one camera with a projector — a device that can emit controlled patterns of light (typically a digital light projector, or DLP). The projector-camera pair defines the same epipolar geometry as a camera-camera pair, with the projector’s image plane serving as a “virtual camera” plane. The key difference: while a camera passively records light, the projector emits it with full knowledge of what is being emitted.

Here is the crucial consequence. When the projector sends a ray of light through a specific pixel $p$ in its virtual image plane, that ray illuminates a unique physical point $P$ in the scene. The camera, observing the scene, captures the reflection of that illuminated point at pixel $p’$ in its image. Because you know exactly what the projector sent ($p$ is fully known), identifying $p’$ in the camera image gives you an immediate, unambiguous correspondence. The matching problem reduces to asking: “where in the camera image can I see the pattern I just projected?” — a far easier question than passive feature matching.


From Points to Lines: The Scanning Stripe Approach

Projecting a single point tells you the 3D location of one surface point. To reconstruct an entire surface, the simplest active stereo strategy is to project a thin vertical stripe (a line of light) across the scene. The stripe illuminates a curve on the object’s surface, which appears as a bright line in the camera image.

If the projector and camera are configured to be rectified (their image rows aligned with the epipolar lines), then the correspondence search collapses to a simple one-dimensional problem: each point on the observed stripe $s’$ in the camera can only correspond to the point on the same horizontal epipolar line in the projector. With correspondences established, every point on the illuminated stripe $S$ is triangulated, recovering a 3D curve on the surface.

By sweeping the stripe laterally across the scene — one stripe position at a time — and repeating the triangulation for each position, the complete visible surface of the object is reconstructed point by point. This is the principle behind laser line scanning, one of the workhorses of industrial metrology and heritage digitization.


The historical pinnacle of this approach came in 2000, when Marc Levoy and his team at Stanford applied a finely calibrated laser scanner to Michelangelo’s Pietà, achieving sub-millimeter accuracy across the entire sculpture. The result was a digital 3D model of extraordinary fidelity — a testament to how powerful active stereo becomes when the system is carefully engineered.

The Calibration of an Active Stereo System

An active stereo system must be calibrated before it can produce accurate measurements. The camera is calibrated first using standard techniques — a checkerboard calibration rig, for instance — to recover its intrinsic parameters and lens distortions. Then, with the camera calibrated, known stripes are projected onto the calibration rig. By observing where these stripes appear in the camera image and matching those observations to the known geometry of the rig, constraints can be established to estimate the projector’s intrinsic and extrinsic parameters (its focal length, principal point, and pose relative to the camera). Once both devices are calibrated, the system is ready to triangulate.


A Cheaper Alternative: Shadow Stripes

What if you cannot afford a high-quality digital projector? An inexpensive but surprisingly effective alternative uses shadows instead of projected light. Place a thin stick between the object and a known light source. The stick’s shadow creates a dark stripe on the object’s surface — functionally equivalent to a projected stripe, but achieved with nothing more than a stick and a lamp.

Moving the stick progressively casts different shadow stripes across the object, and the reconstruction proceeds exactly as in the scanning stripe approach. The method is cheap and requires no specialized equipment beyond a camera, a light source, and a stick. The trade-off is accuracy: the sharpness and position of a shadow stripe is more sensitive to the geometry of the stick, the light source, and the camera, making calibration more demanding and reconstruction less precise.


Single-Shot Reconstruction: Structured Light

The scanning stripe method has a significant practical limitation: it requires the object to be completely still while the stripe sweeps across it. Any motion during the scan produces artifacts. For dynamic scenes — a person moving, a robot manipulating an object, a face making expressions — scanning is far too slow.

The solution is structured light: rather than scanning one stripe at a time, project an entire pattern of multiple distinctively-colored or distinctively-coded stripes simultaneously, illuminating the entire visible surface in a single exposure. If the stripe pattern is designed such that every stripe has a unique color (or unique local code), then the camera can identify which stripe is which from a single image, and all correspondences are established at once.


Figure 3 in the source notes illustrates this: a pattern of differently-colored vertical stripes is projected onto an object, and the camera observes the distorted, color-coded pattern on the surface. By identifying each stripe’s color, correspondences are established across the entire surface simultaneously, and the full 3D shape is recovered from a single projected frame.

This idea powered an iconic consumer product: the original Microsoft Kinect. Rather than visible colored stripes (which would be disturbing in normal use), Kinect used an infrared laser projector to project a pseudo-random dot pattern invisible to the human eye. An infrared camera captured the pattern as it deformed over the scene’s geometry. By matching the deformed pattern back to the known projected pattern, per-pixel depth estimates were computed in real time at video frame rates — enabling body tracking, gesture interfaces, and countless downstream applications.

Part 2: Volumetric Stereo — Turning the Problem Inside Out

A Completely Different Philosophy

Active stereo still relies on a projector-camera geometry that fundamentally resembles traditional stereo — it just makes correspondences easy. Volumetric stereo takes a much more radical departure. Rather than finding correspondences and triangulating forward, it starts with candidate 3D points and asks whether they are consistent with what the cameras observe.

Here is the mental model. Imagine you know that the object you want to reconstruct is sitting inside a glass box — a bounded working volume. Fill that box with a dense 3D grid of tiny cubes called voxels (short for volumetric pixels). Each voxel is a candidate piece of the object. Your task is to figure out which voxels are actually occupied by the object and which are empty space.

For each candidate voxel, project it into all the calibrated cameras and check: does what the cameras see at those projection locations agree with what you would expect if that voxel were part of the object? If yes, keep the voxel. If no, discard it. The surviving voxels, after checking all candidates, form your 3D reconstruction.

This approach elegantly sidesteps the correspondence problem. You never ask “which pixel in image 1 matches which pixel in image 2?” Instead, you ask “is this specific 3D location consistent with all available views?” The consistency check is local to each candidate voxel.

Of course, everything hinges on how you define “consistent.” Different choices lead to different algorithms. We will examine three: space carving, shadow carving, and voxel coloring.

Method 1: Space Carving — Using Silhouettes as Constraints

The Geometric Insight

Space carving begins with a beautiful geometric observation: the silhouette of an object — the boundary of its projection in an image — is a powerful constraint on its 3D shape.

Think about what a silhouette tells you. When you photograph a ball against a white background, the silhouette is a circle. Every 3D point that could possibly produce that circular silhouette must lie inside the visual cone — the cone-shaped region formed by shooting rays from the camera center through every pixel on the silhouette boundary. Any 3D point outside this cone would project outside the silhouette, so it cannot belong to the object.

Now here is the power of multiple views. From camera 1, you compute a visual cone. From camera 2, you compute a different visual cone. Since the object must be inside both cones simultaneously, it must lie in their intersection. Add a third camera, and the object must be in the intersection of three cones. More cameras tighten the estimate.

The intersection of all visual cones from all cameras is called the visual hull. The visual hull is always a conservative upper bound on the object’s shape — the real object fits inside it, but the visual hull may contain regions that are not part of the object. You can think of it as the most the silhouettes can tell you without any other information.


Practical Implementation: Voxels and Projection

In practice, space carving is implemented on a discrete voxel grid:

  1. Initialize the working volume as a full voxel grid, where every voxel is initially marked as “occupied.”
  2. For each camera, extract the silhouette of the object in that image. If the background is controlled — for example, using a green screen — this segmentation is straightforward.
  3. For each voxel, project it into the camera image.
  4. If the voxel’s projection falls outside the silhouette, the voxel cannot be part of the object — remove it (carve it away).
  5. After processing all cameras, the remaining voxels form the visual hull estimate.

The name “space carving” evokes the right mental image: you start with a solid block and progressively chisel away voxels that are inconsistent with each silhouette view, like a sculptor revealing the form hidden inside a block of marble.

An important property of the algorithm is that it is conservative: it never removes a voxel that might genuinely be part of the object (assuming perfect silhouettes). Every removal is justified by the certainty that the voxel falls outside the object’s projection in at least one view. This means the reconstruction always contains the true object — but may contain extra material around it.

Limitations of Space Carving

Space carving is elegant and avoids the correspondence problem entirely, but it has real limitations.

The first is computational cost. The algorithm iterates over every voxel in the grid and projects it into every camera. If you halve the voxel size to double the reconstruction resolution, the number of voxels increases by a factor of $2^3 = 8$ in 3D — a cubic relationship. Fine reconstructions require enormous grids and corresponding computation time. Hierarchical data structures like octrees, which adaptively refine the voxel grid only where needed, can mitigate this.

The second limitation is concavities. Space carving fundamentally cannot reconstruct concave regions of an object’s surface. Why? Consider a bowl viewed from above. The inside of the bowl is a concavity — a region scooped inward. But from any camera that can see the bowl, the silhouette includes the entire bowl including its rim. The visual hull therefore fills in the interior of the bowl, treating it as solid. Carving cannot reach into the concavity without removing material that genuinely belongs to the object.

To see this more precisely: a voxel inside a concavity projects within the silhouette in every view, so space carving keeps it — incorrectly. The algorithm has no way to know the concavity exists based on silhouettes alone. The only concavities that space carving handles correctly are holes through the object (like a donut), where the hole is visible in the silhouette from certain angles.


Method 2: Shadow Carving — Illuminating Concavities

Shadow carving addresses the concavity limitation by introducing an additional source of information: self-shadows.

When an object with a concave region is illuminated from the side, its protruding parts often cast shadows onto the concave area itself. The shape and extent of these self-shadows carry geometric information about the concavity that the silhouette alone cannot provide.

The Setup

The shadow carving setup augments the space carving system with a carefully arranged array of lights at known positions surrounding the camera. The object is placed on a turntable so it can be observed from multiple angles. By turning individual lights on and off in sequence, the object is illuminated from different directions, producing different self-shadow patterns on its surface for each lighting configuration.

The Algorithm

Shadow carving begins by running space carving with the silhouette, producing an initial visual hull that over-estimates the object’s volume. The subsequent shadow carving steps then refine this hull by carving away voxels in concave regions.

For each light source and each camera view, the algorithm identifies the shadow cast by the object in the camera image. This shadow, like the silhouette, defines a visual cone — the “shadow cone” — emanating from the light source through the shadow boundary in the image. The key logical step is subtle but powerful: a voxel that falls inside both the shadow cone of the light source and the visual cone of the camera simultaneously cannot be part of the object. If it were, it would be both visible to the camera (the camera’s visual cone implies it is in the camera’s line of sight within the silhouette) and in shadow (the light’s shadow cone implies it is occluded from the light). The presence of a shadow on the object’s surface implies that something is between the light and the shadowed region — and those “something” voxels can be refined away from the concavity.


By cycling through all lights and all views, shadow carving progressively carves away voxels in concave regions that space carving would have left untouched, producing a tighter estimate of the true object shape.

Trade-offs

Shadow carving shares the cubic scaling of space carving. With $N$ lights, each voxel must be projected into the camera and into each of the $N$ light sources — multiplying the computation by approximately $N + 1$ relative to vanilla space carving.

The method also has material restrictions. It fundamentally relies on detecting sharp, clear shadows in the camera image. Objects with highly reflective surfaces scatter light in complex ways that smear shadow boundaries, making detection unreliable. Similarly, very dark (low-albedo) objects absorb most incident light and produce faint shadows that are difficult to detect against a dark object surface. For such materials, shadow carving degrades significantly.

Method 3: Voxel Coloring — Consistency Through Color

The third volumetric stereo technique, voxel coloring, replaces the geometric consistency check of space carving (silhouette containment) with a photometric one: color consistency.

The Core Idea

The idea is intuitive. If a voxel truly lies on the surface of an object, then projecting that voxel into multiple cameras should yield similar colors in all of them — because they are all looking at the same physical surface point. If the colors are wildly different across views, the voxel is probably not on the surface (perhaps it is in empty space, where different cameras see different background colors projected back to that location).

For each voxel in the working volume, voxel coloring:

  1. Projects the voxel into every camera that has a clear line of sight to it.
  2. Samples the image color at each projection location.
  3. If the sampled colors are mutually consistent (within some threshold), marks the voxel as occupied and assigns it the average color.
  4. If the colors are inconsistent, discards the voxel.


The bonus beyond space carving: the voxels not only capture the object’s shape but also its appearance. The resulting reconstruction is a colored voxel model — simultaneously a geometric and a photometric representation. This makes voxel coloring attractive for applications where texture matters, like cultural heritage digitization or product visualization.

The Lambertian Assumption

Voxel coloring rests on a critical assumption: the object must be Lambertian. A Lambertian surface is one that scatters incoming light uniformly in all directions — a matte surface, like unvarnished wood, rough plaster, or matte paint. The perceived brightness and color of a Lambertian surface is independent of the viewing direction, which is exactly what the color consistency check requires: the same surface point should look the same from camera 1 as from camera 2.

Highly specular (shiny) or reflective objects violate this assumption badly. A polished metal sphere looks different depending on the viewing angle — it reflects the environment, showing different colors to different cameras even though the sphere’s surface material has not changed. For such objects, the color consistency check fails even on voxels that genuinely belong to the object, causing them to be incorrectly discarded.

This is a fundamental physical limitation of photometric consistency methods, not a flaw that can be engineered away without more sophisticated models of surface reflectance.

The Ambiguity Problem and the Visibility Ordering Fix

Vanilla voxel coloring has a subtle but important failure mode: the solution is not necessarily unique. Multiple different configurations of occupied voxels can produce the same projected colors in all cameras. How does this happen?

Consider two voxels on the same camera ray, one behind the other. From that camera’s perspective, the front voxel occludes the back one. If the front voxel’s color matches the scene at that pixel, the algorithm accepts it. But if the front voxel were absent, the back voxel’s color might also match (because the camera would then see a different part of the scene). This ambiguity means multiple solutions can be consistent with the observations.

The fix is to enforce a visibility ordering constraint: process voxels in order from closest to the cameras to farthest. This “front-to-back” traversal ensures that when you evaluate a voxel, all voxels closer to the camera have already been evaluated. If a closer voxel is accepted (occupied), it legitimately occludes the ones behind it — and those occluded voxels are no longer required to pass the color consistency check for cameras that cannot see them. This mimics how real surfaces work: the front of an object blocks the view to the back, and the back need not be consistent with views it is not visible from.

Implementing the visibility ordering requires that the cameras be arranged such that a consistent front-to-back ordering exists for all voxels and all cameras simultaneously. This places a constraint on camera placement that is more restrictive than in space carving — specifically, certain camera configurations where no global ordering exists cannot be handled by this approach.

Comparing the Three Volumetric Methods


The three volumetric methods each occupy a distinct niche, defined by their assumptions, information source, and capabilities:

Space carving uses only silhouettes. It is the simplest and fastest of the three (per view), requires only the ability to segment the object from its background, and produces a conservative visual hull. It cannot recover concavities and degrades when silhouettes are imprecise. Best suited for convex or near-convex objects where silhouette segmentation is easy.

Shadow carving adds self-shadows to the silhouette consistency. It is more expensive (scales as $N+1$ times space carving with $N$ lights) but can recover some concave geometry that space carving misses. It requires a controlled lighting environment and fails for reflective or dark surfaces. Best suited for objects with complex concave geometry under controlled lab conditions.

Voxel coloring uses color consistency instead of silhouette geometry. It captures both shape and texture simultaneously, handles a wider variety of surface geometries than space carving (including concavities, provided they are photometrically distinct), and produces intrinsically textured reconstructions. It requires Lambertian surfaces and a specific camera ordering constraint. Best suited for objects with rich, matte surface texture.

All three are volumetric in the sense that they work within a bounded working volume, making them best suited for isolated object reconstruction rather than large-scale scene reconstruction. None of them replace structure from motion for recovering large environments.

Active Stereo vs. Volumetric Stereo: When to Use What

These two families of techniques address the correspondence problem in entirely different ways, and each excels in different scenarios.


Active stereo — whether scanning stripe, structured light, or infrared dot patterns — is the right choice when you have control of the illumination and need high accuracy on arbitrary surfaces, including those with uniform texture or complex material properties. Industrial inspection systems, dental scanners, and consumer depth cameras (like the Kinect and its successors) all use active stereo precisely because it produces dense, accurate depth maps in challenging conditions. The trade-off is the need for a projector, controlled lighting, and the limitation that the projected pattern can interfere with simultaneously capturing natural-light photographs.

Volumetric stereo is the right choice when you can surround the object with multiple cameras and want a full 3D model rather than a depth map from a single viewpoint. It is particularly natural for object digitization — putting a sculpture or artifact on a turntable and photographing or filming it from all angles. The working volume assumption is naturally satisfied, and the resulting voxel representation can be directly converted to a mesh for rendering or analysis.

In the modern landscape, these approaches complement rather than replace each other. A sophisticated 3D scanning system might use structured light for high-accuracy depth from individual viewpoints, and then use volumetric or structure-from-motion methods to fuse multiple viewpoints into a coherent full-object model.

Conclusion: Rethinking the Problem to Solve It

What makes active and volumetric stereo conceptually satisfying is that they do not merely solve the correspondence problem — they reframe it.

Active stereo eliminates ambiguity by construction: projecting a known pattern ensures that the “which pixel matches which?” question has a trivially readable answer. You do not need to rely on the scene to be textured; you bring your own texture in the form of light. The practical consequences are enormous — from museum-quality digital archives of irreplaceable sculptures to depth-sensing capabilities in everyday consumer devices.

Volumetric stereo takes the inverse approach, questioning the very direction in which the problem is posed. Instead of working forward from image pixels to 3D points, it works backward from candidate 3D points to image consistency. The correspondence problem disappears because you are checking consistency directly in 3D, bypassing the 2D matching step entirely. The three variants — space carving, shadow carving, and voxel coloring — show how much mileage you can extract from different notions of consistency: geometric (silhouette), illumination-based (shadows), and photometric (color).

Taken together, these methods illustrate a broader lesson in computer vision: when a problem seems intractable, sometimes the right response is not a better algorithm for the original formulation, but a reframing of the problem itself. Projecting light to create correspondences, or checking candidate volumes rather than finding matches — both are examples of this creative reframing, and both have proven their worth in the lab and in the real world.

This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 5: Active and Volumetric Stereo, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

If the background is controlled — for example, using a green screen — this segmentation is straightforward. For each voxel, project it into the camera image. If the voxel’s projection falls outside the silhouette, the voxel cannot be part of the object — remove it (carve it away). After processing all cameras, the remaining voxels form the visual hull estimate. The name “space carving” evokes the right mental image: you start with a solid block and progressively chisel away voxels that are inconsistent with each silhouette view, like a sculptor revealing the form hidden inside a block of marble. An important property of the algorithm is that it is conservative: it never removes a voxel that might genuinely be part of the object (assuming perfect silhouettes). Every removal is justified by the certainty that the voxel falls outside the object’s projection in at least one view. This means the reconstruction always contains the true object — but may contain extra material around it. Limitations of Space Carving Space carving is elegant and avoids the correspondence problem entirely, but it has real limitations. The first is computational cost. The algorithm iterates over every voxel in the grid and projects it into every camera. If you halve the voxel size to double the reconstruction resolution, the number of voxels increases by a factor of $2^3 = 8$ in 3D — a cubic relationship. Fine reconstructions require enormous grids and corresponding computation time. Hierarchical data structures like octrees, which adaptively refine the voxel grid only where needed, can mitigate this. The second limitation is concavities. Space carving fundamentally cannot reconstruct concave regions of an object’s surface. Why? Consider a bowl viewed from above. The inside of the bowl is a concavity — a region scooped inward. But from any camera that can see the bowl, the silhouette includes the entire bowl including its rim. The visual hull therefore fills in the interior of the bowl, treating it as solid. Carving cannot reach into the concavity without removing material that genuinely belongs to the object. To see this more precisely: a voxel inside a concavity projects within the silhouette in every view, so space carving keeps it — incorrectly. The algorithm has no way to know the concavity exists based on silhouettes alone. The only concavities that space carving handles correctly are holes through the object (like a donut), where the hole is visible in the silhouette from certain angles. Method 2: Shadow Carving — Illuminating Concavities Shadow carving addresses the concavity limitation by introducing an additional source of information: self-shadows. When an object with a concave region is illuminated from the side, its protruding parts often cast shadows onto the concave area itself. The shape and extent of these self-shadows carry geometric information about the concavity that the silhouette alone cannot provide. The Setup The shadow carving setup augments the space carving system with a carefully arranged array of lights at known positions surrounding the camera. The object is placed on a turntable so it can be observed from multiple angles. By turning individual lights on and off in sequence, the object is illuminated from different directions, producing different self-shadow patterns on its surface for each lighting configuration. The Algorithm Shadow carving begins by running space carving with the silhouette, producing an initial visual hull that over-estimates the object’s volume. The subsequent shadow carving steps then refine this hull by carving away voxels in concave regions. For each light source and each camera view, the algorithm identifies the shadow cast by the object in the camera image. This shadow, like the silhouette, defines a visual cone — the “shadow cone” — emanating from the light source through the shadow boundary in the image. The key logical step is subtle but powerful: a voxel that falls inside both the shadow cone of the light source and the visual cone of the camera simultaneously cannot be part of the object. If it were, it would be both visible to the camera (the camera’s visual cone implies it is in the camera’s line of sight within the silhouette) and in shadow (the light’s shadow cone implies it is occluded from the light). The presence of a shadow on the object’s surface implies that something is between the light and the shadowed region — and those “something” voxels can be refined away from the concavity. By cycling through all lights and all views, shadow carving progressively carves away voxels in concave regions that space carving would have left untouched, producing a tighter estimate of the true object shape. Trade-offs Shadow carving shares the cubic scaling of space carving. With $N$ lights, each voxel must be projected into the camera and into each of the $N$ light sources — multiplying the computation by approximately $N + 1$ relative to vanilla space carving. The method also has material restrictions. It fundamentally relies on detecting sharp, clear shadows in the camera image. Objects with highly reflective surfaces scatter light in complex ways that smear shadow boundaries, making detection unreliable. Similarly, very dark (low-albedo) objects absorb most incident light and produce faint shadows that are difficult to detect against a dark object surface. For such materials, shadow carving degrades significantly. Method 3: Voxel Coloring — Consistency Through Color The third volumetric stereo technique, voxel coloring, replaces the geometric consistency check of space carving (silhouette containment) with a photometric one: color consistency. The Core Idea The idea is intuitive. If a voxel truly lies on the surface of an object, then projecting that voxel into multiple cameras should yield similar colors in all of them — because they are all looking at the same physical surface point. If the colors are wildly different across views, the voxel is probably not on the surface (perhaps it is in empty space, where different cameras see different background colors projected back to that location). For each voxel in the working volume, voxel coloring: Projects the voxel into every camera that has a clear line of sight to it. Samples the image color at each projection location. If the sampled colors are mutually consistent (within some threshold), marks the voxel as occupied and assigns it the average color. If the colors are inconsistent, discards the voxel. The bonus beyond space carving: the voxels not only capture the object’s shape but also its appearance. The resulting reconstruction is a colored voxel model — simultaneously a geometric and a photometric representation. This makes voxel coloring attractive for applications where texture matters, like cultural heritage digitization or product visualization. The Lambertian Assumption Voxel coloring rests on a critical assumption: the object must be Lambertian. A Lambertian surface is one that scatters incoming light uniformly in all directions — a matte surface, like unvarnished wood, rough plaster, or matte paint. The perceived brightness and color of a Lambertian surface is independent of the viewing direction, which is exactly what the color consistency check requires: the same surface point should look the same from camera 1 as from camera 2. Highly specular (shiny) or reflective objects violate this assumption badly. A polished metal sphere looks different depending on the viewing angle — it reflects the environment, showing different colors to different cameras even though the sphere’s surface material has not changed. For such objects, the color consistency check fails even on voxels that genuinely belong to the object, causing them to be incorrectly discarded. This is a fundamental physical limitation of photometric consistency methods, not a flaw that can be engineered away without more sophisticated models of surface reflectance. The Ambiguity Problem and the Visibility Ordering Fix Vanilla voxel coloring has a subtle but important failure mode: the solution is not necessarily unique. Multiple different configurations of occupied voxels can produce the same projected colors in all cameras. How does this happen? Consider two voxels on the same camera ray, one behind the other. From that camera’s perspective, the front voxel occludes the back one. If the front voxel’s color matches the scene at that pixel, the algorithm accepts it. But if the front voxel were absent, the back voxel’s color might also match (because the camera would then see a different part of the scene). This ambiguity means multiple solutions can be consistent with the observations. The fix is to enforce a visibility ordering constraint: process voxels in order from closest to the cameras to farthest. This “front-to-back” traversal ensures that when you evaluate a voxel, all voxels closer to the camera have already been evaluated. If a closer voxel is accepted (occupied), it legitimately occludes the ones behind it — and those occluded voxels are no longer required to pass the color consistency check for cameras that cannot see them. This mimics how real surfaces work: the front of an object blocks the view to the back, and the back need not be consistent with views it is not visible from. Implementing the visibility ordering requires that the cameras be arranged such that a consistent front-to-back ordering exists for all voxels and all cameras simultaneously. This places a constraint on camera placement that is more restrictive than in space carving — specifically, certain camera configurations where no global ordering exists cannot be handled by this approach. Comparing the Three Volumetric Methods The three volumetric methods each occupy a distinct niche, defined by their assumptions, information source, and capabilities: Space carving uses only silhouettes. It is the simplest and fastest of the three (per view), requires only the ability to segment the object from its background, and produces a conservative visual hull. It cannot recover concavities and degrades when silhouettes are imprecise. Best suited for convex or near-convex objects where silhouette segmentation is easy. Shadow carving adds self-shadows to the silhouette consistency. It is more expensive (scales as $N+1$ times space carving with $N$ lights) but can recover some concave geometry that space carving misses. It requires a controlled lighting environment and fails for reflective or dark surfaces. Best suited for objects with complex concave geometry under controlled lab conditions. Voxel coloring uses color consistency instead of silhouette geometry. It captures both shape and texture simultaneously, handles a wider variety of surface geometries than space carving (including concavities, provided they are photometrically distinct), and produces intrinsically textured reconstructions. It requires Lambertian surfaces and a specific camera ordering constraint. Best suited for objects with rich, matte surface texture. All three are volumetric in the sense that they work within a bounded working volume, making them best suited for isolated object reconstruction rather than large-scale scene reconstruction. None of them replace structure from motion for recovering large environments. Active Stereo vs. Volumetric Stereo: When to Use What These two families of techniques address the correspondence problem in entirely different ways, and each excels in different scenarios. Active stereo — whether scanning stripe, structured light, or infrared dot patterns — is the right choice when you have control of the illumination and need high accuracy on arbitrary surfaces, including those with uniform texture or complex material properties. Industrial inspection systems, dental scanners, and consumer depth cameras (like the Kinect and its successors) all use active stereo precisely because it produces dense, accurate depth maps in challenging conditions. The trade-off is the need for a projector, controlled lighting, and the limitation that the projected pattern can interfere with simultaneously capturing natural-light photographs. Volumetric stereo is the right choice when you can surround the object with multiple cameras and want a full 3D model rather than a depth map from a single viewpoint. It is particularly natural for object digitization — putting a sculpture or artifact on a turntable and photographing or filming it from all angles. The working volume assumption is naturally satisfied, and the resulting voxel representation can be directly converted to a mesh for rendering or analysis. In the modern landscape, these approaches complement rather than replace each other. A sophisticated 3D scanning system might use structured light for high-accuracy depth from individual viewpoints, and then use volumetric or structure-from-motion methods to fuse multiple viewpoints into a coherent full-object model. Conclusion: Rethinking the Problem to Solve It What makes active and volumetric stereo conceptually satisfying is that they do not merely solve the correspondence problem — they reframe it. Active stereo eliminates ambiguity by construction: projecting a known pattern ensures that the “which pixel matches which?” question has a trivially readable answer. You do not need to rely on the scene to be textured; you bring your own texture in the form of light. The practical consequences are enormous — from museum-quality digital archives of irreplaceable sculptures to depth-sensing capabilities in everyday consumer devices. Volumetric stereo takes the inverse approach, questioning the very direction in which the problem is posed. Instead of working forward from image pixels to 3D points, it works backward from candidate 3D points to image consistency. The correspondence problem disappears because you are checking consistency directly in 3D, bypassing the 2D matching step entirely. The three variants — space carving, shadow carving, and voxel coloring — show how much mileage you can extract from different notions of consistency: geometric (silhouette), illumination-based (shadows), and photometric (color). Taken together, these methods illustrate a broader lesson in computer vision: when a problem seems intractable, sometimes the right response is not a better algorithm for the original formulation, but a reframing of the problem itself. Projecting light to create correspondences, or checking candidate volumes rather than finding matches — both are examples of this creative reframing, and both have proven their worth in the lab and in the real world. This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 5: Active and Volumetric Stereo, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

entry.title: Camera Models
entry.content:
How Cameras See the World: A Deep Dive into Camera Models for Computer Vision

From pinhole optics to projection matrices — understanding the mathematics and intuition behind how cameras translate 3D reality into 2D images.

Every photograph you have ever taken is, at its core, a mathematical transformation. The rich, three-dimensional world around you — with its depth, texture, and spatial relationships — gets compressed into a flat, two-dimensional grid of pixels. Yet somehow, we look at photographs and instantly reconstruct the 3D scene in our minds. The question that lies at the heart of computer vision is: how do we teach machines to do the same thing?

Before a machine can interpret an image, it needs a precise, mathematical understanding of how that image was formed in the first place. This is the role of camera models — formal descriptions of the geometric and optical process by which a 3D scene becomes a 2D image. Getting this right is foundational to almost everything interesting in computer vision: 3D reconstruction, augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging all depend on accurate camera models underneath the hood.

The Simplest Camera Imaginable: The Pinhole Model

The Core Idea

Imagine you are in a completely dark room, and you poke a tiny hole in one wall. On the opposite wall, you will see a dim, upside-down image of the scene outside projected through that hole. This is a camera obscura — and it is the conceptual ancestor of every camera ever built.

Why does this work? Think about what happens without the hole. Every point on the outside scene radiates light in all directions. Without any filtering, every point on the opposite wall receives light from every point in the scene simultaneously — a chaotic, incoherent mess. The tiny hole acts as a filter: it allows only a single ray of light from each point in the scene to pass through to the wall. Now each location on the wall receives light from exactly one corresponding location in the scene — a clean, one-to-one mapping. The result is a coherent image.


This is the essence of the pinhole camera model. A barrier with a small aperture sits between the 3D scene and the image surface (called the image plane or retinal plane). Only those rays that pass through the aperture reach the image plane. This enforces the crucial one-to-one correspondence between scene points and image points.

The Geometry and the Projection Equation

Let’s make this precise. We set up a coordinate system centered at the pinhole — which we call the optical center \(O\). The three axes of this coordinate system, \(\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{j}\), and \(\mathbf{k}\), define what is known as the camera coordinate system. The axis \(\mathbf{k}\) points perpendicularly toward the image plane, and the line connecting the optical center to the center of the image plane is called the optical axis.

The image plane sits at a distance \(f\) from the pinhole — and this distance is one of the most important parameters in all of camera optics: the focal length.

Now consider a point \(P = [x, y, z]^T\) in 3D space. Where does it land on the image plane? We can work this out using elementary geometry. The ray from \(P\) through the pinhole \(O\) hits the image plane at some point \(P' = [x', y']^T\). Since the triangles formed by the ray on each side of the pinhole are similar, we can write:

\[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f \frac{x}{z} \\ f \frac{y}{z} \end{bmatrix} \tag{1}\]


Here, \(x\) and \(y\) are the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the 3D point, \(z\) is its depth (distance along the optical axis), and \(f\) is the focal length. The fraction \(\frac{x}{z}\) is exactly what you’d expect intuitively: a point that is twice as far away (\(z\) doubles) appears to be half as far from the center of the image (\(x'\) halves). This is the mathematical expression of perspective — the reason train tracks appear to converge in the distance.

Notice the critical nonlinearity: we are dividing by \(z\). This means the mapping from 3D to 2D is not a simple linear transformation — a fact that will have important consequences for how we represent it in matrix form later.

The Aperture Dilemma

The pinhole model assumes the aperture is a mathematical point — infinitely small. In practice, this is impossible to achieve, and there is a fundamental tradeoff hiding here.

If the aperture is very small, the one-to-one mapping is nearly perfect and the image is sharp. But very little light gets through, making the image very dark. If the aperture is enlarged, more light enters, but now each point on the image plane receives rays from multiple scene points — the image blurs. This is the classic tension every photographer knows: aperture size controls both brightness and sharpness, and you cannot have both simultaneously without an additional optical element.


This tradeoff is what motivated the invention of lenses.

Lenses: Solving the Brightness-Sharpness Dilemma

A lens is a piece of shaped glass that refracts (bends) light rays. A convex lens, properly designed and positioned, has a remarkable property: all the light rays emitted by a single scene point $P$, no matter what direction they travel when they hit the lens, are bent so that they all converge to the same image point $P’$ on the image plane.

This is the key insight. Without a lens, only the one ray that happened to be aimed at the tiny pinhole would contribute to forming the image. With a lens, the enormous number of rays radiating from $P$ across the full aperture of the lens all cooperate to illuminate the same image point $P’$. The image becomes dramatically brighter, without sacrificing the clean one-to-one mapping.

Lenses also have a special relationship with parallel rays: all light rays traveling parallel to the optical axis are focused by the lens to converge at a single point called the focal point. The distance from the lens center to the focal point is, again, the focal length $f$.


Using a simple geometric model of lens behavior (known as the paraxial refraction model, or thin lens approximation), one can derive a projection equation similar to the pinhole case:

\[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{z' x}{z} \\ \frac{z' y}{z} \end{bmatrix} \tag{2}\]

The key difference from the pinhole model is that instead of $z’ = f$, we now have $z’ = f + z_0$, where $z_0$ is the distance from the lens to the image plane. This extra term accounts for the fact that the lens refracts rather than simply blocks light.

Depth of Field and Focus

There is one important limitation with lenses: the perfect convergence to a single image point only works for scene points at a specific distance from the lens. Points that are closer or farther will not converge perfectly on the image plane — their rays will hit the plane while still spreading out, creating a blurred disk (called a circle of confusion). The range of distances over which objects appear acceptably sharp is called the depth of field.

This is why portrait photographers use wide apertures (for beautiful background blur) and landscape photographers use narrow apertures (to keep everything sharp from foreground to horizon). The mathematics of depth of field flows directly from the lens model we’ve just described.


Radial Distortion: When Lenses Aren’t Perfect

The paraxial (thin lens) approximation assumes that incoming rays make very small angles with the optical axis, allowing us to substitute $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$. For wide-angle lenses or rays far from the center, this approximation breaks down, and real lenses introduce radial distortion.

Radial distortion causes the image magnification to vary as a function of distance from the optical center. When magnification increases away from the center, straight lines bow outward — this is called pincushion distortion. When magnification decreases away from the center, lines bow inward — this is called barrel distortion, the characteristic wide “fisheye” look. Both arise because different regions of the lens have slightly different effective focal lengths. This is a real-world imperfection that must be accounted for in precise computer vision applications.


From Image Plane to Digital Pixels: The Full Camera Model

The projection equation we derived maps a 3D point to a continuous 2D coordinate on the image plane. But a real digital image is not a continuous plane — it is a discrete grid of pixels, often with a different coordinate origin and possibly different physical units. Bridging this gap requires several additional steps.

Step 1: The Principal Point Offset

The image coordinate system in a pinhole camera has its origin at the principal point $C’$ — the point where the optical axis pierces the image plane, right at the center of the image. But digital images typically place their origin at the top-left or bottom-left corner. The displacement between these two origins is described by two parameters, $c_x$ and $c_y$ (in physical units), and the projection equation becomes:

\[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f \frac{x}{z} + c_x \\ f \frac{y}{z} + c_y \end{bmatrix} \tag{3}\]


Step 2: Converting to Pixels

Points in the image plane are measured in physical units (millimeters, say), but pixels are discrete, dimensionless units. To convert, we introduce two scaling factors: $k$ and $l$, measured in pixels per unit length. These may differ from each other because pixels are not guaranteed to be perfectly square — the aspect ratio depends on the sensor. When $k = l$, we say the camera has square pixels.

We often fold $f$ and the scaling factors together into combined parameters $\alpha = fk$ and $\beta = fl$, giving:

\[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \frac{x}{z} + c_x \\ \beta \frac{y}{z} + c_y \end{bmatrix} \tag{4}\]

Here $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the focal lengths in units of pixels, which is how you will most commonly see them in practice.

Homogeneous Coordinates: Making Division into Multiplication

We now face a mathematical nuisance. The projection $P \to P’$ involves division by $z$, which means it cannot be written as a simple matrix-vector multiplication. Linear algebra is most powerful when we can write everything as $\mathbf{y} = M\mathbf{x}$, but our transformation stubbornly refuses to cooperate — or so it seems.

The elegant solution is a change of representation called homogeneous coordinates.

The idea is beautifully simple: append an extra coordinate. A 2D point $(x, y)$ becomes $(x, y, 1)$ in homogeneous coordinates. More generally, any point $(x, y, w)$ in homogeneous coordinates represents the Euclidean point $(x/w, y/w)$. Going back to Euclidean coordinates simply means dividing through by the last coordinate. And a 3D point $(x, y, z)$ becomes $(x, y, z, 1)$.

This trick allows us to absorb the problematic division into the coordinate system itself. Now we can write the full projection as a matrix-vector product:

\[P'_h = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha x + c_x z \\ \beta y + c_y z \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & \beta & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \tag{5}\]

To recover the actual 2D pixel coordinates, we divide the first two entries by the third: $x’ = (\alpha x + c_x z)/z = \alpha x/z + c_x$, exactly as before. The division happens, but it is now hidden inside the conversion from homogeneous back to Euclidean coordinates.

From here on, all coordinates are assumed to be homogeneous unless stated otherwise.

The Camera Matrix $K$: Packaging the Intrinsic Parameters

We can factor the projection matrix cleanly:

\[P' = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & \beta & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} P = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & \beta & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} I & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} P = K \begin{bmatrix} I & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} P \tag{6}\]

The $3 \times 3$ matrix $K$ is called the camera matrix (or camera intrinsic matrix):

\[K = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & -\alpha \cot\theta & c_x \\ 0 & \frac{\beta}{\sin\theta} & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \tag{7}\]

The angle $\theta$ here accounts for skew — the possibility that the pixel axes are not perfectly perpendicular to each other, typically due to manufacturing imperfections. For most cameras, $\theta = 90°$, so $\cot\theta = 0$ and $\sin\theta = 1$, and the skew term vanishes.

In the general case with skew included, $K$ has exactly 5 degrees of freedom:

  • $\alpha$ and $\beta$: focal lengths in pixel units (2 parameters)
  • $c_x$ and $c_y$: principal point offset (2 parameters)
  • $\theta$ (or equivalently the skew value): pixel axis angle (1 parameter)


These five numbers, collectively called the intrinsic parameters, fully characterize the internal optics of a specific camera. They are properties of the camera itself — they change if you swap the lens or use a different sensor, but not if you point the camera in a different direction.

Extrinsic Parameters: Where Is the Camera in the World?

So far, we have described how a 3D point expressed in camera coordinates gets projected onto the image plane. But the 3D world has its own coordinate system — a world reference frame — that may be completely different from the camera’s local frame.

Think of it this way: a surveyed map of a city defines a world coordinate system. A camera placed somewhere in the city has its own local coordinate system. To project a building’s corner (specified in world coordinates) onto the camera’s image, we first need to convert that building corner from world coordinates to camera coordinates.


This coordinate transformation is captured by a rotation matrix $R$ (a $3 \times 3$ orthogonal matrix with determinant 1) and a translation vector $T$ (a 3D vector). Together they describe the camera’s position and orientation in the world. Given a point $P_w$ in world coordinates, its camera-frame coordinates are:

\[P = \begin{bmatrix} R & T \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} P_w \tag{8}\]

Substituting this into our projection equation gives the complete pipeline from world point to pixel:

\[P' = K \begin{bmatrix} R & T \end{bmatrix} P_w = M P_w \tag{9}\]

The $3 \times 4$ matrix $M = K[R \mid T]$ is called the full projection matrix. It encodes everything about the camera — intrinsic and extrinsic.

$R$ and $T$ are the extrinsic parameters — they describe the camera’s pose in the world, not any intrinsic optical property. They change whenever you move or rotate the camera.

Counting degrees of freedom for the complete projection matrix: 5 from the intrinsic camera matrix $K$, 3 from the rotation $R$ (which can be parameterized by three Euler angles or equivalent), and 3 from the translation $T$ — giving 11 degrees of freedom in total. Remarkably, the entire geometry of a camera in the world can be described by just 11 numbers.

Camera Calibration: Recovering the Camera Parameters from Images

Knowing the projection matrix $M$ precisely is essential for many applications. In robotics, you need to know exactly where a detected object is in 3D space. In augmented reality, you need to overlay virtual objects on the real scene with perfect alignment. In photogrammetry, you reconstruct 3D structure from photographs. All of these require knowing $K$, $R$, and $T$.

The problem of estimating these parameters from images is called camera calibration.

The Setup: A Calibration Rig

The standard approach uses a calibration rig — an object with a known, precisely measured 3D structure. The classic choice is a checkerboard pattern. Because we know the exact geometry of the checkerboard, we know the 3D world coordinates $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ of the grid corners. We then photograph the checkerboard and find the corresponding 2D pixel locations $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ in the image. Each pair $(P_i, p_i)$ is a correspondence.


Setting Up the Linear System


Each correspondence provides two equations. Given the projection $p_i = [u_i, v_i]^T = MP_i$, where $M$ has rows $\mathbf{m}_1^T, \mathbf{m}_2^T, \mathbf{m}_3^T$, we can write:

\[u_i = \frac{\mathbf{m}_1^T P_i}{\mathbf{m}_3^T P_i}, \qquad v_i = \frac{\mathbf{m}_2^T P_i}{\mathbf{m}_3^T P_i}\]

Rearranging to eliminate the denominator:

\(u_i (\mathbf{m}_3^T P_i) - \mathbf{m}_1^T P_i = 0\) \(v_i (\mathbf{m}_3^T P_i) - \mathbf{m}_2^T P_i = 0\)

Stacking these equations for all $n$ correspondences gives a homogeneous linear system:

\[\mathcal{P}\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0} \tag{10}\]

where $\mathbf{m}$ is a vector containing all 12 entries of $M$, and $\mathcal{P}$ is a $2n \times 12$ matrix built from the correspondence data.

Since $M$ has 11 degrees of freedom (and is only determined up to an overall scale), we need at least 6 correspondences to have more equations than unknowns ($2 \times 6 = 12 > 11$). In practice, many more are used to handle measurement noise.

Solving via SVD

The system $\mathcal{P}\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0}$ has a trivial solution ($\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0}$), which is useless. We add the constraint $|\mathbf{m}|^2 = 1$ to prevent this, and solve the minimization:

\[\min_{\mathbf{m}} \|\mathcal{P}\mathbf{m}\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{m}\|^2 = 1 \tag{11}\]

This is solved elegantly using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). If $\mathcal{P} = UDV^T$, the solution is the last column of $V$ — the right singular vector corresponding to the smallest singular value. This vector is the direction in the null space of $\mathcal{P}$ that best approximates a zero, given noisy data.

Extracting Intrinsics and Extrinsics

After reshaping $\mathbf{m}$ back into the matrix $M$, we know $M$ up to a global scale factor $\rho$. From this scaled matrix, we can algebraically recover the individual intrinsic and extrinsic parameters:

\[\rho = \pm \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{a}_3\|}, \quad c_x = \rho^2 (\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_3), \quad c_y = \rho^2 (\mathbf{a}_2 \cdot \mathbf{a}_3)\] \[\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(- \frac{(\mathbf{a}_1 \times \mathbf{a}_3) \cdot (\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3)}{\|\mathbf{a}_1 \times \mathbf{a}_3\| \cdot \|\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3\|}\right)\] \[\alpha = \rho^2 \|\mathbf{a}_1 \times \mathbf{a}_3\| \sin\theta, \quad \beta = \rho^2 \|\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3\| \sin\theta \tag{12}\]

The extrinsic parameters follow from:

\[\mathbf{r}_3 = \rho \mathbf{a}_3, \quad \mathbf{r}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3}{\|\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3\|}, \quad \mathbf{r}_2 = \mathbf{r}_3 \times \mathbf{r}_1, \quad T = \rho K^{-1} \mathbf{b} \tag{13}\]

where $\mathbf{a}_1^T, \mathbf{a}_2^T, \mathbf{a}_3^T$ are the rows of the $3 \times 3$ left submatrix of $M$, and $\mathbf{b}$ is its last column.

Degenerate Configurations

Not every set of correspondences will work. If all the calibration points happen to lie on a single plane, the system becomes degenerate and cannot be solved — there are infinitely many projection matrices consistent with planar point sets. More generally, degenerate configurations arise whenever points lie on the intersection curve of two quadric surfaces. This is why checkerboard calibration rigs are designed to be three-dimensional, often captured from multiple angles, ensuring the points span 3D space.

Handling Distortion in Calibration

Real lenses deviate from the ideal pinhole model. The most common imperfection is radial distortion, which warps the image in a way that is symmetric around the optical center.

We can model this distortion with an isotropic scaling factor $\lambda$ that depends on the distance from the image center:

\[Q P_i = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\lambda} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\lambda} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} M P_i = p_i \tag{14}\]

Unfortunately, introducing this distortion model makes the calibration system nonlinear — $\lambda$ itself may be a function of image position, so we can no longer use SVD directly. However, there is a useful observation: radial distortion does not affect the ratio $u_i / v_i$, since both coordinates are divided by the same $\lambda$. This allows us to estimate the first two rows of $M$ using a linear system (solvable by SVD), and then recover the third row and $\lambda$ through a simpler nonlinear optimization. The full nonlinear distortion problem is thus reduced to a more tractable form.

Alternative Camera Models: When Perspective Is Overkill

The perspective (pinhole) camera model is accurate, but computationally rich. In some scenarios, simpler approximations are sufficient and much more convenient to work with.

The Weak Perspective Model

Imagine you are photographing an object that is relatively small compared to its distance from the camera. In this case, the variation in depth across the object — from its nearest point to its farthest — is tiny compared to the overall distance $z_0$. Under these conditions, the perspective division by $z$ can be replaced by division by the fixed reference depth $z_0$, giving a constant magnification across the entire object:

\[x' = \frac{f'}{z_0} x, \qquad y' = \frac{f'}{z_0} y\]

The ratio $m = f’/z_0$ is just a single magnification constant. This is the weak perspective model. It simplifies the projection matrix so that the bottom row becomes $[0\ 0\ 0\ 1]$ rather than the variable expression in the full perspective model. The beautiful consequence is that the nonlinearity of projection disappears entirely — the transformation becomes a simple linear magnification, independent of depth.

The projection in the weak perspective model takes the clean form:

\[P' = MP = \begin{bmatrix} m_1 \\ m_2 \\ m_3 \end{bmatrix} P = \begin{bmatrix} m_1 P \\ m_2 P \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \tag{15}\]

Each image coordinate is just a linear function of the 3D point coordinates. No division, no depth dependence. This makes many algorithms dramatically simpler while remaining accurate for small, distant objects.

The Orthographic Projection Model

Pushing the approximation even further, if the camera is conceptually placed at infinity (the optical center recedes infinitely far from the scene), all projection rays become parallel and perpendicular to the image plane. The image coordinates are simply the $x$ and $y$ coordinates of the 3D point, with no scaling whatsoever:

\[x' = x, \qquad y' = y\]

This is the orthographic projection model (also called affine projection). Depth is completely ignored — an object 10 meters away looks exactly the same as one 100 meters away, as long as their $x$ and $y$ coordinates match. This is clearly unrealistic for most photography, but it is the standard model in architectural drawings and engineering schematics, where preserving true proportions without perspective distortion is the goal.

Think of a blueprint: a room drawn in orthographic projection allows you to directly measure distances on paper and map them to real-world distances with a single scale factor. No correction for perspective is needed.


Rigid Transformations: The Mathematics of Moving Through Space

Underpinning the entire discussion is a family of geometric operations called rigid transformations — transformations that preserve distances and angles. The key ones are rotation, translation, and scaling.

Rotation

A rotation in 3D can be described as a combination of rotations around the three coordinate axes. The rotation matrices for each axis are:

\[R_x(\alpha) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ 0 & \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}, \quad R_y(\beta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\beta & 0 & \sin\beta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\beta & 0 & \cos\beta \end{bmatrix}\] \[R_z(\gamma) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\gamma & -\sin\gamma & 0 \\ \sin\gamma & \cos\gamma & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

These are called Euler angle rotations. To rotate first around $z$, then $y$, then $x$, you apply the matrix product $R_x R_y R_z$. Note that rotation matrices are orthogonal ($R^T R = I$) with determinant 1 — they perfectly preserve lengths and angles.

One important subtlety: Euler angles can lead to a problem called gimbal lock, where certain configurations cause a loss of a rotational degree of freedom (two of the three axes become aligned, reducing 3D rotation to a 2D one). This is why many robotics and aerospace systems use alternative representations like quaternions.

Translation and Combined Transformations

Translation simply shifts a point by a vector $\mathbf{t} = [t_x, t_y, t_z]^T$:

\[P' = P + \mathbf{t}\]

In homogeneous coordinates, this can be written as a matrix multiplication using the translation matrix:

\[T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & t_z \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

The power of homogeneous coordinates is that we can now chain rotations, translations, and scalings together by simply multiplying matrices — every transformation in the pipeline becomes a matrix, and the full pipeline is their product. The final combined transformation matrix for rotating by $R$, scaling by $S$, and translating by $\mathbf{t}$ is:

\[T_{\text{combined}} = \begin{bmatrix} RS & \mathbf{t} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

All of these rotation, translation, and scaling operations are examples of affine transformations (they preserve parallel lines). The full perspective projection, however, is a projective transformation, distinguished by the fact that the bottom row of the matrix is not simply $[0\ 0\ 0\ 1]$ — this is precisely the term responsible for the perspective division by $z$.

Putting It All Together: The Complete Projection Pipeline

Let’s step back and appreciate the full picture. Starting from a 3D point $P_w$ in the world:

  1. Rigid transformation ($R$, $T$): Convert from world coordinates to camera coordinates. This accounts for where the camera is positioned and how it is oriented in the world.

  2. Perspective projection: Project the 3D camera-frame point onto the 2D image plane using the focal length, encoding the geometry of the pinhole (or lens).

  3. Intrinsic calibration ($K$): Apply the camera matrix to account for pixel scaling ($\alpha$, $\beta$), principal point offset ($c_x$, $c_y$), and potential skew ($\theta$). This converts from idealized image plane coordinates to actual pixel coordinates in the digital image.

The entire pipeline is:

\[P' = K \begin{bmatrix} R & T \end{bmatrix} P_w \tag{16}\]

This compact equation is arguably the most important formula in all of computer vision. Every photograph ever taken by a digital camera is, in some sense, an instance of this equation being applied to a 3D scene.

Why This All Matters: Practical Implications

Understanding camera models is not academic abstraction — it has immediate, concrete consequences for any system that works with images.

In autonomous vehicles, the cameras mounted on the car must have precisely known intrinsic and extrinsic parameters so that detected objects (pedestrians, traffic lights, road markings) can be accurately localized in 3D space relative to the vehicle. A calibration error of even a few pixels can translate to errors of tens of centimeters in 3D position estimates — potentially catastrophic at highway speeds.

In augmented reality, virtual objects must be rendered with the same perspective, focal length, and distortion as the real camera. If the intrinsic parameters are slightly off, virtual objects will seem to “float” or “slide” relative to the real world as you move your head. The illusion depends entirely on precise calibration.

In 3D reconstruction (photogrammetry, structure-from-motion), multiple photographs taken from different angles are used to reconstruct the 3D geometry of a scene. This is only possible because each photograph encodes the projection geometry through the camera model, and those projections can be inverted — with sufficient correspondences — to recover the 3D structure.

In medical imaging, calibration matters when cameras are used in surgical robotics or endoscopy, where the precise mapping between image coordinates and physical space can mean the difference between a successful procedure and a dangerous mistake.

Conclusion: A Mathematical Window on the World

We began with a simple observation — a pinhole in a barrier creates an image — and ended with a complete mathematical framework for understanding how any camera maps the 3D world to a 2D image. Along the way, we discovered that:

The pinhole model gives us the fundamental perspective projection $x’ = fx/z$, capturing the essence of how depth creates apparent size. Lenses resolve the practical tension between brightness and sharpness, while introducing distortions that must be modeled and corrected. The camera matrix $K$ packages the five intrinsic parameters that characterize a camera’s optics, while the rotation $R$ and translation $T$ describe its pose in the world. Homogeneous coordinates provide the algebraic sleight-of-hand that lets us write the nonlinear perspective projection as a linear matrix multiplication. Camera calibration recovers all these parameters from images of known calibration targets, using the elegant machinery of SVD. And simplified models like weak perspective and orthographic projection offer useful approximations when the full perspective model is more than we need.

Every time you take a photo, run a face detection algorithm, or watch an autonomous car navigate traffic, this mathematics is silently at work — encoding the geometry of light, space, and optics into the numbers that machines can reason about. Understanding camera models is, in a real sense, understanding how computers learn to see.

This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 1: Camera Models, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.
entry.summary: How Cameras See the World: A Deep Dive into Camera Models for Computer Vision From pinhole optics to projection matrices — understanding the mathematics and intuition behind how cameras translate 3D reality into 2D images. Every photograph you have ever taken is, at its core, a mathematical transformation. The rich, three-dimensional world around you — with its depth, texture, and spatial relationships — gets compressed into a flat, two-dimensional grid of pixels. Yet somehow, we look at photographs and instantly reconstruct the 3D scene in our minds. The question that lies at the heart of computer vision is: how do we teach machines to do the same thing? Before a machine can interpret an image, it needs a precise, mathematical understanding of how that image was formed in the first place. This is the role of camera models — formal descriptions of the geometric and optical process by which a 3D scene becomes a 2D image. Getting this right is foundational to almost everything interesting in computer vision: 3D reconstruction, augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging all depend on accurate camera models underneath the hood. The Simplest Camera Imaginable: The Pinhole Model The Core Idea Imagine you are in a completely dark room, and you poke a tiny hole in one wall. On the opposite wall, you will see a dim, upside-down image of the scene outside projected through that hole. This is a camera obscura — and it is the conceptual ancestor of every camera ever built. Why does this work? Think about what happens without the hole. Every point on the outside scene radiates light in all directions. Without any filtering, every point on the opposite wall receives light from every point in the scene simultaneously — a chaotic, incoherent mess. The tiny hole acts as a filter: it allows only a single ray of light from each point in the scene to pass through to the wall. Now each location on the wall receives light from exactly one corresponding location in the scene — a clean, one-to-one mapping. The result is a coherent image. This is the essence of the pinhole camera model. A barrier with a small aperture sits between the 3D scene and the image surface (called the image plane or retinal plane). Only those rays that pass through the aperture reach the image plane. This enforces the crucial one-to-one correspondence between scene points and image points. The Geometry and the Projection Equation Let’s make this precise. We set up a coordinate system centered at the pinhole — which we call the optical center \(O\). The three axes of this coordinate system, \(\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{j}\), and \(\mathbf{k}\), define what is known as the camera coordinate system. The axis \(\mathbf{k}\) points perpendicularly toward the image plane, and the line connecting the optical center to the center of the image plane is called the optical axis. The image plane sits at a distance \(f\) from the pinhole — and this distance is one of the most important parameters in all of camera optics: the focal length. Now consider a point \(P = [x, y, z]^T\) in 3D space. Where does it land on the image plane? We can work this out using elementary geometry. The ray from \(P\) through the pinhole \(O\) hits the image plane at some point \(P' = [x', y']^T\). Since the triangles formed by the ray on each side of the pinhole are similar, we can write: \[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f \frac{x}{z} \\ f \frac{y}{z} \end{bmatrix} \tag{1}\] Here, \(x\) and \(y\) are the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the 3D point, \(z\) is its depth (distance along the optical axis), and \(f\) is the focal length. The fraction \(\frac{x}{z}\) is exactly what you’d expect intuitively: a point that is twice as far away (\(z\) doubles) appears to be half as far from the center of the image (\(x'\) halves). This is the mathematical expression of perspective — the reason train tracks appear to converge in the distance. Notice the critical nonlinearity: we are dividing by \(z\). This means the mapping from 3D to 2D is not a simple linear transformation — a fact that will have important consequences for how we represent it in matrix form later. The Aperture Dilemma The pinhole model assumes the aperture is a mathematical point — infinitely small. In practice, this is impossible to achieve, and there is a fundamental tradeoff hiding here. If the aperture is very small, the one-to-one mapping is nearly perfect and the image is sharp. But very little light gets through, making the image very dark. If the aperture is enlarged, more light enters, but now each point on the image plane receives rays from multiple scene points — the image blurs. This is the classic tension every photographer knows: aperture size controls both brightness and sharpness, and you cannot have both simultaneously without an additional optical element. This tradeoff is what motivated the invention of lenses. Lenses: Solving the Brightness-Sharpness Dilemma A lens is a piece of shaped glass that refracts (bends) light rays. A convex lens, properly designed and positioned, has a remarkable property: all the light rays emitted by a single scene point $P$, no matter what direction they travel when they hit the lens, are bent so that they all converge to the same image point $P’$ on the image plane. This is the key insight. Without a lens, only the one ray that happened to be aimed at the tiny pinhole would contribute to forming the image. With a lens, the enormous number of rays radiating from $P$ across the full aperture of the lens all cooperate to illuminate the same image point $P’$. The image becomes dramatically brighter, without sacrificing the clean one-to-one mapping. Lenses also have a special relationship with parallel rays: all light rays traveling parallel to the optical axis are focused by the lens to converge at a single point called the focal point. The distance from the lens center to the focal point is, again, the focal length $f$. Using a simple geometric model of lens behavior (known as the paraxial refraction model, or thin lens approximation), one can derive a projection equation similar to the pinhole case: \[P' = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{z' x}{z} \\ \frac{z' y}{z} \end{bmatrix} \tag{2}\] The key difference from the pinhole model is that instead of $z’ = f$, we now have $z’ = f + z_0$, where $z_0$ is the distance from the lens to the image plane. This extra term accounts for the fact that the lens refracts rather than simply blocks light. Depth of Field and Focus There is one important limitation with lenses: the perfect convergence to a single image point only works for scene points at a specific distance from the lens. Points that are closer or farther will not converge perfectly on the image plane — their rays will hit the plane while still spreading out, creating a blurred disk (called a circle of confusion). The range of distances over which objects appear acceptably sharp is called the depth of field. This is why portrait photographers use wide apertures (for beautiful background blur) and landscape photographers use narrow apertures (to keep everything sharp from foreground to horizon). The mathematics of depth of field flows directly from the lens model we’ve just described. Radial Distortion: When Lenses Aren’t Perfect The paraxial (thin lens) approximation assumes that incoming rays make very small angles with the optical axis, allowing us to substitute $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$. For wide-angle lenses or rays far from the center, this approximation breaks down, and real lenses introduce radial distortion. Radial distortion causes the image magnification to vary as a function of distance from the optical center. When magnification increases away from the center, straight lines bow outward — this is called pincushion distortion. When magnification decreases away from the center, lines bow inward — this is called barrel distortion, the characteristic wide “fisheye” look. Both arise because different regions of the lens have slightly different effective focal lengths. This is a real-world imperfection that must be accounted for in precise computer vision applications.
