Two eyes, two cameras, or one camera moved between two shots can all exploit this principle. But to do so rigorously, we need a mathematical framework that describes exactly how the geometry of two viewpoints constrains what we can see and where. That framework is epipolar geometry. It is one of the foundational pillars of computer vision and 3D reconstruction, and its elegance lies in this: without knowing where a 3D point is, and without even knowing the properties of the cameras involved, epipolar geometry tells us that if a point appears at a specific pixel in one image, it can only appear somewhere along a specific line in the other image. This “epipolar constraint” turns an overwhelming 2D search problem into a 1D one, and it unlocks a chain of algorithms for matching images, estimating camera geometry, and ultimately reconstructing the 3D world. The Limits of a Single View Before diving into the geometry of two cameras, it is worth understanding precisely why one image isn’t enough. When a camera projects the 3D world onto a flat image sensor, it performs a projection along rays. Every point along a ray from the camera center through a pixel maps to the same pixel. Depth — the distance along that ray — is simply lost. This is the intrinsic ambiguity of perspective projection. This ambiguity creates visual illusions that are trivially resolved by a second viewpoint. A famous class of such illusions involves forced perspective photography: a person appears to be holding up the Leaning Tower of Pisa because their hand and the tower, at vastly different depths, happen to project onto the same image region. Viewed from a second camera at a different angle, the deception collapses immediately. The spatial relationship between the person and the tower is unambiguous from two views. The mathematical goal, then, is to formalize what a pair of images tells us that a single image cannot. Part 1: The Epipolar Geometry Setup The Five Key Elements Imagine two cameras — call their optical centers $O_1$ and $O_2$ — both observing the same 3D point $P$. The point $P$ projects to pixel $p$ in the first image and pixel $p’$ in the second image. This simple scenario generates a beautifully structured geometry involving five elements: The baseline is the line segment connecting the two camera centers $O_1$ and $O_2$. Think of it as the physical separation between the two cameras. The epipolar plane is the triangle formed by the two camera centers and the 3D point $P$: the plane passing through $O_1$, $O_2$, and $P$. Every corresponding point pair $(p, p’)$ defines its own epipolar plane, but they all share the baseline. The epipoles $e$ and $e’$ are where the baseline pierces each image plane. In physical terms, $e$ is where camera $O_2$ would appear if it were visible to camera $O_1$ (and vice versa). The epipoles are the projections of each camera center into the other camera’s image. The epipolar lines are the intersections of the epipolar plane with each image plane. In each image, the epipolar line passes through the corresponding image point ($p$ or $p’$) and through the epipole. All epipolar lines in a given image fan out from the same epipole. The Epipolar Constraint — Why It Matters Here is the central insight. Suppose you are given the pixel location $p$ in the first image, and you want to find the corresponding pixel $p’$ in the second image (i.e., the pixel that depicts the same 3D point $P$). Without any geometric knowledge, you would have to search every pixel in the second image — an exhaustive 2D search. That’s computationally expensive, especially for high-resolution images. Epipolar geometry reduces this search to a single line. Because $P$, $O_1$, and $O_2$ all lie in the epipolar plane, the projection of $P$ into the second camera ($p’$) must lie on the intersection of that epipolar plane with the second image plane — the epipolar line. Knowing $p$ in the first image (along with the camera geometry) uniquely determines the epipolar line in the second image. The search for $p’$ is reduced from a 2D area to a 1D line. This matters enormously in practice. Stereo matching, 3D reconstruction, and structure-from-motion all rely fundamentally on the epipolar constraint to make correspondence search tractable. A Special Case: Parallel Cameras A particularly elegant special case arises when the two image planes are parallel to each other, with the baseline running horizontally between them. In this configuration, the baseline never intersects either image plane (it runs parallel to them), so the epipoles are pushed to infinity. The epipolar lines become perfectly horizontal — parallel to the $u$-axis of each image. The consequence is beautifully simple: if a point appears at row $v$ in the first image, its corresponding point in the second image is guaranteed to appear at the same row $v$. The search is reduced from a 2D area to a single row. This is the ideal configuration for stereo cameras, and it is the target of a process called image rectification, which we’ll discuss at length later. Part 2: The Essential Matrix — Encoding Geometry for Calibrated Cameras Building the Constraint Let’s now derive the mathematical form of the epipolar constraint. We begin with the simplest case: canonical cameras, where both cameras have identity intrinsic matrices ($K = K’ = I$). This means image coordinates are the same as coordinates in the camera’s reference frame — we’ve removed the complication of focal length, pixel size, and principal point for now. We place the first camera at the origin, so its projection matrix is simply $M = [I \mid 0]$. The second camera is offset by a rotation $R$ and translation $T$, giving $M’ = [R^T \mid -R^T T]$. Now, consider the 3D point $P$ and its projections $p$ (in camera 1) and $p’$ (in camera 2). Since these are canonical cameras, $p$ and $p’$ are actual 3D ray directions, not pixel coordinates. The location of $p’$ expressed in camera 1’s reference frame is $Rp’ + T$. Because $P$, $O_1$, and $O_2$ all lie in the epipolar plane, two vectors that lie in that plane are $T$ (from $O_1$ to $O_2$) and $Rp’ + T$ (from $O_1$ to $P$). Their cross product $T \times (Rp’ + T) = T \times Rp’$ is normal to the epipolar plane. Since $p$ also lies in the epipolar plane, it must be perpendicular to this normal: \[p^T \cdot [T \times (Rp')] = 0\] Introducing the Cross Product Matrix To make this algebraically cleaner, we use a standard trick from linear algebra: the cross product of any vector $a$ with another vector $b$ can be written as a matrix-vector multiplication: \[a \times b=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_z & a_y \\ a_z & 0 & -a_x \\ -a_y & a_x & 0 \end{bmatrix} b=[a_\times] b\] The matrix $[a_\times]$ is called the cross product matrix (or skew-symmetric matrix) of $a$. Using this notation, the epipolar constraint becomes: \[p^T [T_\times] R p' = 0\] The Essential Matrix The matrix $E = [T_\times] R$ is called the Essential Matrix. The epipolar constraint takes the remarkably compact form: \[p^T E p' = 0\] This $3 \times 3$ matrix encodes everything about the relative geometry between the two cameras — the rotation $R$ and translation $T$ — in a single object. Let’s unpack what it can do. Given the Essential matrix and a point $p$ in the first image, the epipolar line in the second image is $\ell’ = E^T p$. Conversely, given $p’$ in the second image, the epipolar line in the first image is $\ell = E p’$. You can verify this: if $p’$ lies on $\ell’$, then $p’^T \ell’ = p’^T E^T p=(p^T E p’)^T = 0$ ✓. The Essential matrix also has a special relationship with the epipoles. Since every epipolar line in the second image passes through the epipole $e’$, and $e’$ lies on every epipolar line, we have $E e’ = 0$ and $E^T e=0$. The epipoles are in the null space of $E$ and $E^T$ respectively. Structurally, $E$ has 5 degrees of freedom (the rotation $R$ contributes 3, the translation direction $T/|T|$ contributes 2 — we can only recover the direction of translation, not its scale, from the images alone), it has rank 2 (one singular value is zero, corresponding to the null space direction of the epipole), and it is always singular. Part 3: The Fundamental Matrix — Epipolar Geometry Without Calibration Beyond Canonical Cameras The Essential matrix is elegant, but it assumes we know the intrinsic calibration matrices $K$ and $K’$ of both cameras. In many real-world scenarios — photographs downloaded from the internet, images from unknown cameras, historical photos — we don’t have access to calibration information. Can we still reason about epipolar geometry? Yes. The answer is the Fundamental Matrix, the generalization of the Essential matrix to uncalibrated cameras. Recall that for non-canonical cameras, the projection matrices are $M = K[I \mid 0]$ and $M’ = K’[R^T \mid -R^T T]$. We can “undo” the calibration by defining $p_c = K^{-1} p$ and $p’_c = K’^{-1} p’$ — these are the image coordinates that would be observed if the cameras were canonical. The Essential matrix constraint then gives: \[p_c^T [T_\times] R p'_c = 0\] \[\Rightarrow \quad p^T K^{-T} [T_\times] R K'^{-1} p' = 0\] The matrix sandwiched between $p^T$ and $p’$ is the Fundamental Matrix: \[F = K'^{-T} [T_\times] R K^{-1}\] And the epipolar constraint in the uncalibrated case is: \[p^T F p' = 0\] What the Fundamental Matrix Encodes The Fundamental matrix is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with 7 degrees of freedom. (It has 9 entries, determined only up to scale, reducing to 8; and the constraint $\det F=0$ reduces it to 7.) It encodes not just the relative camera geometry ($R$, $T$) but also the intrinsic parameters of both cameras ($K$, $K’$). Like the Essential matrix, $F$ maps points to epipolar lines: $\ell’ = F^T p$ gives the epipolar line in the second image, and $\ell = F p’$ gives the epipolar line in the first. The epipoles satisfy $F^T e=0$ and $F e’ = 0$. The most powerful aspect of $F$ is this: if we can estimate the Fundamental matrix directly from image correspondences (without knowing $K$, $R$, or $T$), then we gain the ability to compute epipolar lines for any pair of images, purely from observed pixel coordinates. This is what makes the Fundamental matrix the workhorse of uncalibrated stereo and structure-from-motion. Part 4: The Eight-Point Algorithm — Estimating F from Correspondences The Setup The Eight-Point Algorithm (proposed by Longuet-Higgins in 1981, extended by Hartley in 1995) answers a practical question: given two photographs of the same scene, with no knowledge of the cameras, how can we estimate the Fundamental matrix? The input is a set of corresponding point pairs $(p_i, p’_i)$: pixel locations in both images that depict the same 3D point. Finding such correspondences is itself a challenge (handled by feature detection algorithms like SIFT or ORB), but assuming we have them, each correspondence gives us one equation from the epipolar constraint: \[p_i^T F p'_i = 0\] If we write $p_i = (u_i, v_i, 1)$ and $p’i = (u’_i, v’_i, 1)$ and expand $F$ into its 9 entries $F{jk}$, this constraint becomes a linear equation in the entries of $F$: \[\begin{bmatrix} u_i u'_i & v'_i u_i & u_i & u'_i v_i & v_i v'_i & v_i & u'_i & v'_i & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} F_{11} \\ F_{12} \\ F_{13} \\ F_{21} \\ F_{22} \\ F_{23} \\ F_{31} \\ F_{32} \\ F_{33} \end{bmatrix} = 0\] Each correspondence contributes one such row. Stacking $N$ correspondences gives the matrix equation: \[W \mathbf{f} = 0\] where $W$ is an $N \times 9$ matrix and $\mathbf{f}$ is the 9-vector of $F$’s entries. Since $F$ is determined only up to scale, we have 8 effective unknowns, requiring at least 8 correspondences — hence the name “Eight-Point Algorithm.” Solving via SVD With 8 or more correspondences, this is a homogeneous linear system. The solution is found via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD): we decompose $W = U \Sigma V^T$ and take the column of $V$ corresponding to the smallest singular value as the solution $\mathbf{f}$, then reshape it into the $3 \times 3$ matrix $\hat{F}$. However, $\hat{F}$ may have rank 3 (full rank), whereas the true Fundamental matrix must have rank 2 (it must be singular, since the epipoles lie in its null space). We enforce this by finding the best rank-2 approximation: decompose $\hat{F} = U\Sigma V^T$, set the smallest singular value to zero, and recompose: \[F = U \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \Sigma_2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} V^T\] This is the closest rank-2 matrix to $\hat{F}$ in the Frobenius norm sense — the mathematically optimal way to enforce the rank constraint. Why the Naive Version Fails — and the Normalized Fix The standard Eight-Point Algorithm as described has a significant practical problem: it produces poor results on real images. The culprit is numerical ill-conditioning. Modern cameras have image coordinates in the range of thousands of pixels — for example, a 1920×1080 image has $u$ values up to 1920 and $v$ values up to 1080. When these large numbers are multiplied together to form the entries of $W$ (products like $u_i u’_i$ reach values in the millions), the resulting matrix has wildly different scales across its columns. SVD requires a well-conditioned matrix — one where the singular values are not spread across many orders of magnitude. With raw pixel coordinates, $W$ is badly conditioned, and the SVD solution is dominated by numerical noise rather than the true geometric constraint. The fix is normalization, introduced by Hartley. Before constructing $W$, we apply a coordinate transformation to each image independently, satisfying two conditions: Translation: shift the coordinate origin to the centroid of all the image points. Scaling: rescale so that the average distance from the origin to the points is $\sqrt{2}$ pixels. These two operations together ensure that the point coordinates are roughly on the order of 1, making $W$ well-conditioned for SVD. The transformation can be represented as a matrix $T$ (and $T’$ for the second image), giving normalized coordinates $q_i = T p_i$ and $q’_i = T’ p’_i$. We then run the Eight-Point Algorithm on the normalized coordinates to get $F_q$ — the Fundamental matrix for normalized coordinates. Finally, we de-normalize to recover the Fundamental matrix in the original pixel coordinate system: \[F = T'^T F_q T\] This normalized version works reliably in practice, reducing the point-to-epipolar-line error from tens of pixels (with the naive version) to sub-pixel accuracy. Part 5: Image Rectification — Achieving the Ideal Parallel Configuration Why Rectification Matters Recall the ideal stereo configuration: two cameras with parallel image planes, where corresponding points share the same row coordinate. In this configuration, stereo matching reduces to a 1D horizontal search. But in practice, two cameras are rarely in this perfect configuration — they might be angled toward each other, tilted, or mounted with slight misalignment. Image rectification is the process of computing and applying projective transformations (homographies) to both images so that the result looks as if the images were taken by a parallel stereo rig. The epipolar lines become horizontal, and corresponding points end up on the same row. The Rectification Strategy The key insight is that the epipoles encode the “badness” of the alignment. In an ideally rectified pair, the epipoles are at infinity along the horizontal axis. So the rectification goal is: find homographies $H_1$ and $H_2$ to apply to the two images such that the epipoles are mapped to horizontal infinity. We don’t need to know $K$, $R$, or $T$ to do this. We start from the Fundamental matrix (estimated via the Normalized Eight-Point Algorithm) and the correspondences, and proceed as follows. Step 1: Find the epipoles. From the Fundamental matrix, we know that each epipolar line $\ell_i = F^T p_i$ passes through the epipole $e’$. In theory, all epipolar lines intersect at $e’$. In practice (due to measurement noise), they don’t all pass through exactly the same point, so we find $e’$ by minimizing the least-squares fitting error — essentially solving the system: \[\begin{bmatrix} \ell_1^T \\ \vdots \\ \ell_n^T \end{bmatrix} e' = 0\] via SVD. The epipole $e$ in the first image is found analogously. Step 2: Construct $H_2$ to rectify the second image. We want to map the epipole $e’$ to a point at infinity on the horizontal axis. This is accomplished through a three-step sequence of transformations: First, translate the image so its center is at the coordinate origin: \[T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\text{width}/2 \\ 0 & 1 & -\text{height}/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] Then, rotate to place the translated epipole $Te’$ onto the horizontal axis. If $Te’ = (e’_1, e’_2, 1)$, the rotation is: \[R = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \frac{e'_1}{\sqrt{e'^2_1 + e'^2_2}} & \alpha \frac{e'_2}{\sqrt{e'^2_1 + e'^2_2}} & 0 \\ -\alpha \frac{e'_2}{\sqrt{e'^2_1 + e'^2_2}} & \alpha \frac{e'_1}{\sqrt{e'^2_1 + e'^2_2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] where $\alpha = \text{sign}(e’_1)$ ensures the epipole ends up on the positive horizontal axis. After rotation, the epipole is at some finite point $(f, 0, 1)$. To send it to infinity, we apply the projective transformation: \[G = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1/f & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] This maps the point $(f, 0, 1)$ to $(f, 0, 0)$ — a point at infinity in the horizontal direction. Finally, translate back: \[H_2 = T^{-1} G R T\] Step 3: Construct $H_1$ for the first image. We can’t apply $H_2$ independently to both images — the horizontal alignment of corresponding points would be destroyed. We need $H_1$ to be chosen such that corresponding points $(p_i, p’_i)$ end up on the same row after applying $H_1$ and $H_2$ respectively. The matching homography has the form: \[H_1 = H_A H_2 M\] where $M$ is derived from the Fundamental matrix as $M = [e]_\times F + e v^T$ for some vector $v$ (in practice, $v^T = (1,1,1)$ works well), and $H_A$ is a matrix of the form: \[H_A = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] The three parameters $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$ are found by least-squares. We compute the transformed points $\hat{p}_i = H_2 M p_i$ and $\hat{p}’_i = H_2 p’_i$, and then solve the least-squares problem: \[\arg\min_a \sum_i (a_1 \hat{x}_i + a_2 \hat{y}_i + a_3 - \hat{x}'_i)^2\] This is a standard linear least-squares system $Wa = b$, easily solved by standard methods. Once $a$ is found, $H_A$ is determined and $H_1 = H_A H_2 M$ is complete. The result: applying $H_1$ to the first image and $H_2$ to the second produces a rectified stereo pair where every pair of corresponding points lies on the same horizontal scan line. Part 6: Conceptual Synthesis — The Full Picture It is worth stepping back to appreciate the conceptual architecture of what we have built. The epipolar constraint $p^T F p’ = 0$ is a single bilinear equation relating two image points that depict the same 3D point. It is the fundamental equation of stereo vision. Everything else in this framework is built around computing $F$ (or its calibrated counterpart $E$) and exploiting the constraint it encodes. The Essential matrix $E$ and Fundamental matrix $F$ are related by the intrinsic camera matrices: $F = K’^{-T} E K^{-1}$. The Essential matrix is the “pure geometry” version, capturing only the relative rotation and translation. The Fundamental matrix is the “complete” version, baking in the cameras’ intrinsics as well. When the cameras are known (calibrated), use $E$; when they’re not, use $F$. The Eight-Point Algorithm (in its normalized form) is the canonical method for estimating $F$ from scratch. It requires only pixel correspondences — no calibration targets, no known 3D structure, no camera specifications. The geometric information latent in the relative positions of matching features across two images is sufficient to determine the entire epipolar geometry. Rectification is the practical payoff. By remapping both images into the parallel-camera configuration, we convert the problem of stereo matching — finding corresponding pixels across two arbitrary images — into a structured, efficient 1D search problem. This is the prerequisite for stereo depth estimation, the technology behind autonomous vehicle perception, AR/VR depth sensing, and dense 3D reconstruction from stereo pairs. There is also a deeper philosophical point here. The Fundamental matrix encodes, in a $3 \times 3$ matrix with 7 degrees of freedom, the entire geometric relationship between two cameras and the scene they observe — without any explicit knowledge of the 3D scene structure. This is a form of structure-from-motion bootstrapping: from the statistics of which pixels in two images match each other, we recover the spatial arrangement of the cameras themselves. Two photographs know things about each other, and about the world that made them, that neither photograph knows alone. Conclusion: The Geometry of a Stereo Pair Epipolar geometry is, at its core, the mathematics of having two eyes. It formalizes the intuition that two views of a scene contain vastly more information than the sum of their parts — not because each view is more informative individually, but because the relationship between the views encodes 3D structure. The epipolar plane, baseline, epipoles, and epipolar lines form a geometric vocabulary that describes how a 3D point’s projections across two cameras are constrained. The Essential matrix makes this constraint algebraic for calibrated cameras; the Fundamental matrix extends it to the uncalibrated case. The Eight-Point Algorithm (especially in its normalized form) gives us a practical and surprisingly clean way to estimate $F$ from raw pixel correspondences. And image rectification translates all this theory into the computationally convenient parallel-camera form that makes stereo matching efficient in practice. From a single equation — $p^T F p’ = 0$ — flows an entire pipeline capable of calibrating cameras, matching images, localizing objects in 3D space, and reconstructing scenes from scratch. It is a testament to the power of geometric thinking in computer vision, and a reminder that even a pair of flat photographs contains, encoded in the geometry of their pixels, a rich and recoverable model of the three-dimensional world. This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 3: Epipolar Geometry, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

entry.title: Fitting and Matching
entry.content:
Finding Structure in Noise: A Deep Dive into Fitting and Matching

From least squares to RANSAC to the Hough transform — how computer vision algorithms find clean geometric structure hidden inside messy, real-world data.

Introduction: The Universal Problem of Finding Patterns

Every time a self-driving car detects a lane boundary, or a panorama app stitches two photos together, or a robot arm identifies an object to pick up, the same fundamental challenge arises: how do you find a clean, structured model inside data that is noisy, imprecise, and full of distractions?

This is the fitting problem. You have a set of observed data points, and you want to find the parameters of a geometric model — a line, a plane, a homography, a fundamental matrix — that best explains what you see. The data will never be perfect. Real measurements are noisy. Sensors make errors. And often, a significant fraction of your data points are outliers — observations that are simply wrong, resulting from sensor glitches, misidentified features, or spurious detections that have nothing to do with the structure you are trying to find.


The difference between a working vision system and a broken one often comes down entirely to how well it handles this fitting problem. A method that crumbles in the presence of outliers is not a method you can deploy in the real world. The story of fitting in computer vision is a story of progressively smarter strategies for dealing with the messy reality of data.

In this article, we will develop three major fitting strategies from the ground up: least squares (the classical approach, powerful but fragile), RANSAC (a randomized method that is remarkably robust), and the Hough transform (a clever change of perspective that turns fitting into a voting problem). Each solves a different piece of the puzzle, and together they form a toolkit that appears throughout modern computer vision.

Part 1: Least Squares — The Classical Foundation

What Are We Trying to Do?

Let us begin with the simplest instantiation of the fitting problem: fitting a line to a set of 2D points.

You have $N$ data points ${(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N$ that approximately lie along a straight line, but not perfectly — each point is displaced from the true line by some small amount of noise. You want to find the line parameters that give the best fit.

The naive approach would be to find a line that passes exactly through some of the points, but this ignores most of the data and is extremely sensitive to which specific points you choose. The principled approach is to use all the data simultaneously, defining a global measure of goodness-of-fit and minimizing it.

Ordinary Least Squares: Minimizing Vertical Errors

The most classical fitting criterion is least squares. For a line $y = mx + b$, the model prediction for input $x_i$ is $\hat{y}_i = mx_i + b$. The residual for point $i$ is the difference between the observed $y_i$ and the predicted $\hat{y}_i$:

\[r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - mx_i - b\]


Least squares finds the parameters $m$ and $b$ that minimize the total squared residual:

\[E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - mx_i - b)^2\]

Squaring the residuals serves two purposes: it makes the criterion differentiable (allowing calculus-based optimization), and it ensures that positive and negative errors do not cancel each other out. It also has a deeper statistical justification — it is the maximum likelihood estimator when the noise on each observation is independent and Gaussian.

Deriving the Solution

The power of least squares is that it has a closed-form solution — no iteration required, just a matrix inversion. To see why, rewrite the error in compact matrix notation.

Define the vector of observations $\mathbf{y} = [y_1, \ldots, y_N]^T$, the parameter vector $\mathbf{w} = [m, b]^T$, and the design matrix:

\[X = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ x_N & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

Then the error becomes $E = |\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}|^2$. Expanding and taking the gradient with respect to $\mathbf{w}$:

\[\nabla_\mathbf{w} \|\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}\|^2 = -2X^T\mathbf{y} + 2X^TX\mathbf{w}\]

Setting this equal to zero yields the famous normal equations:

\[X^TX\mathbf{w} = X^T\mathbf{y}\]

When $X$ has full column rank — meaning no two rows are proportional — the matrix $X^TX$ is invertible, and the solution is:

\[\mathbf{w} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}\]

The quantity $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ is called the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $X$, often written $X^+$. It appears throughout linear algebra as the go-to tool for solving overdetermined systems (more equations than unknowns) in the least-squares sense.

The Problem with Vertical Lines: Moving to Total Least Squares

The formulation above measures errors only in the vertical ($y$) direction. The residual $y_i - \hat{y}_i$ asks: “how far is the point from the line in the $y$-direction?” This is asymmetric — it treats $x$ as an exact independent variable and $y$ as the noisy one.

This asymmetry causes a practical disaster: the method completely fails for vertical or near-vertical lines. If the true line is nearly vertical, the slope $m$ becomes enormous (or technically undefined for a perfectly vertical line), leading to numerical instability.

The fix is to switch to a symmetric line parameterization: $ax + by + c = 0$, where the vector $\vec{n} = (a, b)$ is the normal to the line. This form can represent lines of any orientation, including vertical (just set $b = 0$).


In this parameterization, the distance from a point $(x_i, y_i)$ to the line is the perpendicular distance — the shortest possible distance, measured at right angles to the line. This is given by:

\[d_i = \frac{|ax_i + by_i + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}\]

The proof is simple. The distance from a point $P = (x_i, y_i)$ to a line $ax + by + c = 0$ is the length of the vector from $P$ to its nearest point $Q$ on the line, which is the component of $\overrightarrow{QP}$ along the unit normal $\hat{n} = (a,b)/|(a,b)|$. Working through the dot product gives exactly the formula above.

The new error criterion — total least squares — minimizes the sum of squared perpendicular distances:

\[E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (ax_i + by_i + c)^2 \quad \text{subject to } a^2 + b^2 = 1\]

The constraint $a^2 + b^2 = 1$ normalizes the line, ensuring the distance formula is valid and making the solution unique up to sign.

Solving Total Least Squares via SVD

Solving the constrained total least squares problem requires a bit more elegance than ordinary least squares. The key insight is that the optimal line must pass through the centroid of the data, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.

To see why, notice that the error $E$ can be decomposed using the Pythagorean theorem. Any candidate line passing through a point $(x_0, y_0)$ other than the centroid can be improved by shifting it to pass through the centroid instead — the shifted line always reduces the total error. This can be shown rigorously: defining the residuals around an arbitrary center $(x_0, y_0)$ versus the centroid, one obtains $E(a, b, x_0, y_0) \geq E(a, b, \bar{x}, \bar{y})$ with equality only when $(x_0, y_0)$ is the centroid.

With the constraint that the line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, we can eliminate $c$ by substituting $c = -a\bar{x} - b\bar{y}$, and center the data by computing $\tilde{x}_i = x_i - \bar{x}$, $\tilde{y}_i = y_i - \bar{y}$. The error simplifies to:

\[E = \left\| \begin{pmatrix} \tilde{x}_1 & \tilde{y}_1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \tilde{x}_N & \tilde{y}_N \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} \right\|^2 = \|X\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{subject to } \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 1\]

This is a classic constrained least-norm problem: minimize $|X\mathbf{w}|^2$ subject to $|\mathbf{w}|^2 = 1$. The solution comes directly from the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of $X = U \Sigma V^T$.

To minimize $|X\mathbf{w}|^2 = |\Sigma V^T \mathbf{w}|^2$ (using the fact that $U$ is orthonormal and preserves norms), set $\mathbf{v} = V^T\mathbf{w}$. The problem becomes minimizing $|\Sigma \mathbf{v}|^2$ subject to $|\mathbf{v}|^2 = 1$. The diagonal matrix $\Sigma$ scales each component of $\mathbf{v}$ by the corresponding singular value $\sigma_i$. To minimize the result, point $\mathbf{v}$ entirely in the direction of the smallest singular value — i.e., $\mathbf{v} = [0, 1]^T$ (the last standard basis vector, since singular values are sorted in descending order).

Recovering $\mathbf{w} = V\mathbf{v}$ gives: the optimal line normal is the last column of $V$ in the SVD of the centered data matrix. This elegant result says that total least squares finds the direction of minimum variance in the data — the direction along which the data varies least, which is perpendicular to the best-fit line.


This SVD interpretation has a beautiful geometric meaning: SVD finds the principal axes of the data cloud, and total least squares picks the axis of least spread as the line normal.

Why Least Squares Breaks Down: The Outlier Problem

Both ordinary and total least squares share a critical vulnerability: outliers. An outlier is a data point that lies far from the true structure — perhaps due to a sensor glitch, a misidentified feature match, or a measurement from a completely different structure in the scene.

The quadratic error $C(u_i) = u_i^2$ means that an outlier with residual $u_i = 10$ contributes $100$ to the error, while a typical inlier with residual $u_i = 1$ contributes only $1$. The outlier’s contribution is a hundred times larger. In minimizing the total error, the algorithm devotes enormous effort to satisfying the outlier, pulling the fitted model away from the majority of correct points. One bad point can ruin everything.


A natural response is to use a robust cost function that grows more slowly for large residuals. One example is:

\[C(u_i, \sigma) = \frac{u_i^2}{\sigma^2 + u_i^2}\]

When $u_i$ is small (inlier), $C \approx u_i^2 / \sigma^2$ — this behaves like squared error, penalizing deviations from the model. When $u_i$ is large (outlier), $C \to 1$ — the cost saturates, capping the damage any single outlier can do.


The parameter $\sigma$ — the scale parameter — controls the transition between “treated as inlier” and “treated as outlier.” A large $\sigma$ behaves nearly like standard least squares. A small $\sigma$ treats almost everything as an outlier and fits only the very closest points. Choosing $\sigma$ well is essential but non-trivial; it typically requires some knowledge of the noise scale.

Because robust cost functions are nonlinear, they cannot be minimized in closed form. Instead, the standard approach is to start with the least-squares solution as initialization, then iteratively minimize the robust objective using gradient-based methods until convergence.

Part 2: RANSAC — Robust Fitting Through Random Sampling

A Different Philosophy Entirely

Robust cost functions approach the outlier problem by down-weighting suspicious points. RANSAC — RAndom SAmple Consensus — takes a completely different approach: rather than trying to fit all the data while mitigating outlier influence, it finds the subset of the data that is most consistent with some model and fits only that subset.

The intuition is powerful and practical. If you have 100 data points and 40 are outliers, there exists a large “inlier set” of 60 points that all agree on the same underlying model. If you could identify which points belong to the inlier set, standard least squares on those 60 points would give an excellent fit. The challenge is finding that inlier set without knowing the model, and finding the model without knowing the inlier set. RANSAC breaks this circularity with a randomized approach.

The Algorithm

RANSAC for line fitting works as follows. Suppose we have $N$ points that we believe mostly lie along a single line, with some outliers scattered randomly.

Step 1 — Sample: Randomly choose the minimum number of points needed to define the model. For a line, this is exactly 2 points. (For a homography, it would be 4 point correspondences. For a fundamental matrix, it would be 8.)

Step 2 — Fit: Fit the model to the sampled points. For two points, there is exactly one line through them.

Step 3 — Evaluate: Count the inliers — all data points within a distance threshold $\delta$ of the fitted model. Formally, the inlier set is: \(P = \{(x_i, y_i) \mid r((x_i, y_i), \mathbf{w}) < \delta\}\) where $r$ is the residual (perpendicular distance to the line) and $\delta$ is a pre-chosen tolerance. The outlier set is simply everything not in $P$.

Step 4 — Repeat: Go back to Step 1 with a new random sample. Do this for $n$ iterations.

Step 5 — Return: Return the model corresponding to the largest inlier set found across all iterations. Optionally, refit the model using least squares on the entire final inlier set for a more accurate estimate.


Think of RANSAC like a detective canvassing witnesses. Rather than trying to extract a story that reconciles every account (including the unreliable ones), the detective finds the largest group of witnesses whose stories are mutually consistent, and builds the case from those.

How Many Iterations Do You Need?

The key question is: how many iterations $n$ are sufficient to be confident that at least one of your random samples contains only inliers?

Let $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ be the fraction of outliers in the data, and let $s$ be the minimum sample size (for a line, $s = 2$). The probability that a single randomly drawn sample of size $s$ contains all inliers is:

\[(1 - \epsilon)^s\]

The probability that a single sample contains at least one outlier is:

\[1 - (1 - \epsilon)^s\]

The probability that all $n$ samples contain at least one outlier (i.e., we never get a clean sample) is:

\[\left(1 - (1 - \epsilon)^s\right)^n\]

So the probability that at least one of the $n$ samples is clean is:

\[p = 1 - \left(1 - (1 - \epsilon)^s\right)^n\]

Solving for $n$ to achieve a desired success probability $p$:

\[n = \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log\left(1 - (1 - \epsilon)^s\right)}\]

This is a crucial formula. Let us build intuition with some numbers. If 50% of your data are outliers ($\epsilon = 0.5$), fitting a line ($s = 2$), and you want 99% confidence ($p = 0.99$):

\[n = \frac{\log(0.01)}{\log(1 - 0.25)} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.288} \approx 16\]


Just 16 iterations are sufficient! RANSAC is remarkably efficient because even with many outliers, the probability of drawing a clean small sample in repeated trials grows quickly. The formula also reveals when RANSAC becomes expensive: when the model requires a large minimum sample size $s$, or when the outlier fraction $\epsilon$ is very high, the required $n$ grows rapidly.

What Makes RANSAC Special

RANSAC has a combination of properties that make it uniquely suited to computer vision:

It is general — the same algorithm structure applies to any parametric model. Change the sampling step and the fitting step, and you have RANSAC for homographies, fundamental matrices, circles, planes, or any other geometric model. In practice, RANSAC is the standard preprocessing step before computing homographies or fundamental matrices from feature point matches, precisely because the matches always contain false matches (outliers) that would corrupt standard least squares.

It is interpretable — after running RANSAC, you have an explicit inlier set and an explicit outlier set. You know which points the algorithm believes are consistent with the model, and which are not. This transparency is valuable in debugging and analysis.

It is robust to high outlier rates — as long as there is a sufficiently large inlier set, RANSAC will find it even when outliers dominate the data.

The main limitations are that $\delta$ (the inlier threshold) and $n$ (the iteration count) need to be specified, RANSAC is probabilistic (there is always a small chance of failure), and when outlier rates are extreme (above roughly 80-90%), the required iteration count explodes.

Part 3: The Hough Transform — Voting in Parameter Space

A Completely Different Way of Thinking About Fitting

Both least squares and RANSAC work by proposing a model and checking how many points agree with it. The Hough transform takes yet another approach — it is fundamentally a voting procedure, and it expresses a profound duality between image space and parameter space.

The core insight is this: rather than asking “what line fits these points?”, flip the question around and ask “what lines are consistent with each individual point?” Each point has an opinion about all possible lines that could pass through it. If you let every point vote for all lines it is consistent with, then the line that the most points agree on will accumulate the most votes. That line is your answer.

The Image-to-Parameter Duality

Let us make this precise for lines of the form $y = mx + n$ (using $n$ for the intercept to avoid confusion with the iteration count).

A single point $(x_i, y_i)$ in image space lies on every line $y = mx + n$ satisfying $y_i = m x_i + n$, or equivalently:

\[n = -x_i m + y_i\]

This is a line in parameter space $(m, n)$ — a linear relationship between the possible slope $m$ and intercept $n$ values. Every $(m, n)$ pair on this line in parameter space corresponds to a line $y = mx + n$ in image space that passes through $(x_i, y_i)$.

Now consider two image points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$. Each maps to a line in parameter space. If these two points lie on the same image line with parameters $(m’, n’)$, then both parameter-space lines pass through the same point $(m’, n’)$. In other words, the two lines in parameter space intersect at the parameters of the true fitting line.


This is the central magic of the Hough transform: collinear points in image space become concurrent lines in parameter space. Finding a line that fits many points is equivalent to finding a point in parameter space where many lines intersect — a peak in a 2D accumulator.

The Practical Algorithm

In practice, the Hough voting procedure works as follows:

  1. Divide the parameter space into a discrete grid of cells, each cell corresponding to a range of $(m, n)$ values. Initialize all cell counts to zero.
  2. For each data point $(x_i, y_i)$, compute all parameter-space cells $(m, n)$ that satisfy $n = -x_im + y_i$ (approximately, snapping to the nearest grid cell), and increment each such cell by 1.
  3. After processing all data points, find the cell with the highest count. The corresponding $(m, n)$ values are the parameters of the best-fit line.

Each point contributes at most one vote per candidate line — hence the “voting” interpretation. Points that lie near a true line will vote heavily for the corresponding parameter-space cell. Random outliers will spread their votes diffusely across many cells, never concentrating enough to form a peak.

One attractive property of the Hough transform is that it naturally handles multiple structures in the data. If the scene contains two lines, there will be two peaks in parameter space. Each peak corresponds to one line, and the votes for each peak come from the points on that line. This is something standard least squares fundamentally cannot do — it fits a single model to everything. RANSAC can handle multiple structures by running sequentially (fit one model, remove its inliers, repeat), but the Hough transform detects all of them simultaneously.

The Problem with Slope-Intercept Parameters: Unbounded Space

There is a significant practical problem with using $(m, n)$ as the parameter space: the slope $m$ is unbounded. A nearly vertical line has $m \to \pm\infty$, making it impossible to allocate a finite grid. This is the same problem we encountered with ordinary least squares.

The solution is to switch to the polar parameterization of lines:

\[x\cos(\theta) + y\sin(\theta) = \rho\]

In this representation:

  • $\rho$ is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line — bounded by the maximum distance between any two points in the dataset, which for an image of width $W$ and height $H$ is at most $\sqrt{W^2 + H^2}$.
  • $\theta$ is the angle of the line’s normal vector with respect to the $x$-axis — bounded in $[0, \pi)$.

Both parameters are finite, so the parameter space grid is finite. Every line, regardless of orientation, is representable.

With the polar parameterization, a single image point $(x_i, y_i)$ corresponds not to a straight line in parameter space, but to a sinusoidal curve:

\[\rho = x_i \cos(\theta) + y_i \sin(\theta)\]

For different values of $\theta$, this traces out a sinusoid in the $(\theta, \rho)$ plane. Collinear image points produce sinusoids that all pass through the same $(\theta, \rho)$ point — the intersection corresponds to the parameters of the common line.


The voting procedure is otherwise identical: for each data point, trace the sinusoid in the $(\theta, \rho)$ grid and increment all touched cells; after processing all points, find the peak.

Handling Noise and Choosing Grid Resolution

A key practical parameter in the Hough transform is the grid cell size $w$. Noisy data points that theoretically should lie on the same line will, in practice, trace sinusoids that do not intersect at exactly one point but rather form a small cluster of nearby intersections. A grid cell that is too fine will have these votes scattered across several cells, producing no clear peak. A coarser grid bins these nearby votes together, producing a clean peak.

But coarser grids introduce their own problem: cells that are too large will merge the votes of two genuinely different nearby lines, blurring them into a single broad peak and losing the ability to distinguish the lines. This is the classical resolution-precision trade-off: fine grids give precise answers but are sensitive to noise; coarse grids tolerate noise but lose precision.


In the presence of truly uniform noise — points scattered randomly everywhere with no underlying structure — the Hough space will be covered with spurious peaks of roughly equal height, and no single candidate line will achieve a decisive majority. The Hough transform, like all fitting methods, requires that the signal-to-noise ratio be sufficient for the structure to be detectable.

Putting It All Together: When to Use Which Method

These three fitting strategies are not competing alternatives — they are complementary tools, each suited to different conditions.


Ordinary least squares is the right starting point when your data is relatively clean and you have a direct, linear parameterization of the model. It is fast, produces a unique solution, and has a beautiful closed-form expression. It is the backbone of camera calibration, homography computation, and fundamental matrix estimation — but always in combination with a robustification step.

Total least squares with SVD is needed when the error should be measured symmetrically (e.g., fitting lines, planes, or subspaces), or whenever the minimum-norm solution to an underdetermined system is needed. The SVD solution appears throughout computer vision: PCA for dimensionality reduction, the eight-point algorithm for the fundamental matrix, the DLT algorithm for homographies. Understanding total least squares via SVD is understanding the backbone of geometric fitting.

RANSAC is the right tool when the data contains a significant fraction of gross outliers that least squares cannot handle — which is nearly always the case in practical feature matching across images. Standard practice in image stitching, visual odometry, and 3D reconstruction is to use RANSAC to find a clean inlier set, then apply least squares to that inlier set for the final parameter estimate. The combination is highly robust and broadly applicable.

The Hough transform shines when you want to detect multiple structures simultaneously without committing to how many there are, when the data might not be organized into explicit correspondences, or when you want a method that is inherently tolerant of missing data and partial occlusion. It is particularly powerful for detecting lines in edge images (as in lane detection), circles (as in iris detection), and any shape that can be parameterized compactly. Its main cost is memory and computation for the parameter space accumulator.

Conclusion: The Art and Mathematics of Model Fitting

The progression from least squares to RANSAC to the Hough transform tells a coherent story about how algorithms can be made more and more robust to the messiness of real data.

Least squares is optimal when the world cooperates — when noise is small, Gaussian, and free of outliers. It is the right answer to the question “what if all my data is trustworthy?” The mathematics is elegant: the normal equations, the pseudoinverse, SVD — a toolkit of remarkable power and generality that extends far beyond line fitting to virtually every parametric model in computer vision.

Robust cost functions acknowledge that the world does not always cooperate, and try to give outliers less influence without discarding them. They are a continuous, gradient-friendly compromise between trusting all data and ignoring suspicious data.

RANSAC takes the more aggressive stance of deciding which data to trust, based on consensus. By repeatedly hypothesizing a model from a tiny random sample and asking how many points agree, it navigates the chicken-and-egg problem of needing good data to find the model and needing the model to identify good data. The probabilistic analysis gives a clear, principled way to choose how many iterations are enough.

The Hough transform reframes the fitting problem entirely. Instead of asking “what model fits the data?” it asks each data point “what models are you consistent with?” and aggregates the answers. The duality between image space and parameter space — points become lines, lines become points — is one of the most elegant ideas in classical computer vision, and the extension to polar coordinates makes it a practical workhorse for line and shape detection.

Mastering these methods is not just about knowing their formulas. It is about developing the intuition for why each one is designed the way it is — what failure mode in the previous method each new technique was designed to overcome, and what assumptions each one relies on. That design intuition is what allows you to choose the right tool for the problem at hand, and to adapt these classical methods to new challenges as they arise.

This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 6: Fitting and Matching, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.
entry.summary: Finding Structure in Noise: A Deep Dive into Fitting and Matching From least squares to RANSAC to the Hough transform — how computer vision algorithms find clean geometric structure hidden inside messy, real-world data. Introduction: The Universal Problem of Finding Patterns Every time a self-driving car detects a lane boundary, or a panorama app stitches two photos together, or a robot arm identifies an object to pick up, the same fundamental challenge arises: how do you find a clean, structured model inside data that is noisy, imprecise, and full of distractions? This is the fitting problem. You have a set of observed data points, and you want to find the parameters of a geometric model — a line, a plane, a homography, a fundamental matrix — that best explains what you see. The data will never be perfect. Real measurements are noisy. Sensors make errors. And often, a significant fraction of your data points are outliers — observations that are simply wrong, resulting from sensor glitches, misidentified features, or spurious detections that have nothing to do with the structure you are trying to find. The difference between a working vision system and a broken one often comes down entirely to how well it handles this fitting problem. A method that crumbles in the presence of outliers is not a method you can deploy in the real world. The story of fitting in computer vision is a story of progressively smarter strategies for dealing with the messy reality of data. In this article, we will develop three major fitting strategies from the ground up: least squares (the classical approach, powerful but fragile), RANSAC (a randomized method that is remarkably robust), and the Hough transform (a clever change of perspective that turns fitting into a voting problem). Each solves a different piece of the puzzle, and together they form a toolkit that appears throughout modern computer vision. Part 1: Least Squares — The Classical Foundation What Are We Trying to Do? Let us begin with the simplest instantiation of the fitting problem: fitting a line to a set of 2D points. You have $N$ data points ${(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N$ that approximately lie along a straight line, but not perfectly — each point is displaced from the true line by some small amount of noise. You want to find the line parameters that give the best fit. The naive approach would be to find a line that passes exactly through some of the points, but this ignores most of the data and is extremely sensitive to which specific points you choose. The principled approach is to use all the data simultaneously, defining a global measure of goodness-of-fit and minimizing it. Ordinary Least Squares: Minimizing Vertical Errors The most classical fitting criterion is least squares. For a line $y = mx + b$, the model prediction for input $x_i$ is $\hat{y}_i = mx_i + b$. The residual for point $i$ is the difference between the observed $y_i$ and the predicted $\hat{y}_i$: \[r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - mx_i - b\] Least squares finds the parameters $m$ and $b$ that minimize the total squared residual: \[E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - mx_i - b)^2\] Squaring the residuals serves two purposes: it makes the criterion differentiable (allowing calculus-based optimization), and it ensures that positive and negative errors do not cancel each other out. It also has a deeper statistical justification — it is the maximum likelihood estimator when the noise on each observation is independent and Gaussian. Deriving the Solution The power of least squares is that it has a closed-form solution — no iteration required, just a matrix inversion. To see why, rewrite the error in compact matrix notation. Define the vector of observations $\mathbf{y} = [y_1, \ldots, y_N]^T$, the parameter vector $\mathbf{w} = [m, b]^T$, and the design matrix: \[X = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ x_N & 1 \end{pmatrix}\] Then the error becomes $E = |\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}|^2$. Expanding and taking the gradient with respect to $\mathbf{w}$: \[\nabla_\mathbf{w} \|\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}\|^2 = -2X^T\mathbf{y} + 2X^TX\mathbf{w}\] Setting this equal to zero yields the famous normal equations: \[X^TX\mathbf{w} = X^T\mathbf{y}\] When $X$ has full column rank — meaning no two rows are proportional — the matrix $X^TX$ is invertible, and the solution is: \[\mathbf{w} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}\] The quantity $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ is called the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $X$, often written $X^+$. It appears throughout linear algebra as the go-to tool for solving overdetermined systems (more equations than unknowns) in the least-squares sense. The Problem with Vertical Lines: Moving to Total Least Squares The formulation above measures errors only in the vertical ($y$) direction. The residual $y_i - \hat{y}_i$ asks: “how far is the point from the line in the $y$-direction?” This is asymmetric — it treats $x$ as an exact independent variable and $y$ as the noisy one. This asymmetry causes a practical disaster: the method completely fails for vertical or near-vertical lines. If the true line is nearly vertical, the slope $m$ becomes enormous (or technically undefined for a perfectly vertical line), leading to numerical instability. The fix is to switch to a symmetric line parameterization: $ax + by + c=0$, where the vector $\vec{n} = (a, b)$ is the normal to the line. This form can represent lines of any orientation, including vertical (just set $b = 0$). In this parameterization, the distance from a point $(x_i, y_i)$ to the line is the perpendicular distance — the shortest possible distance, measured at right angles to the line. This is given by: \[d_i = \frac{|ax_i + by_i + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}\] The proof is simple. The distance from a point $P = (x_i, y_i)$ to a line $ax + by + c=0$ is the length of the vector from $P$ to its nearest point $Q$ on the line, which is the component of $\overrightarrow{QP}$ along the unit normal $\hat{n} = (a,b)/|(a,b)|$. Working through the dot product gives exactly the formula above. The new error criterion — total least squares — minimizes the sum of squared perpendicular distances: \[E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (ax_i + by_i + c)^2 \quad \text{subject to } a^2 + b^2 = 1\] The constraint $a^2 + b^2 = 1$ normalizes the line, ensuring the distance formula is valid and making the solution unique up to sign. Solving Total Least Squares via SVD Solving the constrained total least squares problem requires a bit more elegance than ordinary least squares. The key insight is that the optimal line must pass through the centroid of the data, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. To see why, notice that the error $E$ can be decomposed using the Pythagorean theorem. Any candidate line passing through a point $(x_0, y_0)$ other than the centroid can be improved by shifting it to pass through the centroid instead — the shifted line always reduces the total error. This can be shown rigorously: defining the residuals around an arbitrary center $(x_0, y_0)$ versus the centroid, one obtains $E(a, b, x_0, y_0) \geq E(a, b, \bar{x}, \bar{y})$ with equality only when $(x_0, y_0)$ is the centroid. With the constraint that the line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, we can eliminate $c$ by substituting $c = -a\bar{x} - b\bar{y}$, and center the data by computing $\tilde{x}_i = x_i - \bar{x}$, $\tilde{y}_i = y_i - \bar{y}$. The error simplifies to: \[E = \left\| \begin{pmatrix} \tilde{x}_1 & \tilde{y}_1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \tilde{x}_N & \tilde{y}_N \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} \right\|^2 = \|X\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{subject to } \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 1\] This is a classic constrained least-norm problem: minimize $|X\mathbf{w}|^2$ subject to $|\mathbf{w}|^2 = 1$. The solution comes directly from the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of $X = U \Sigma V^T$. To minimize $|X\mathbf{w}|^2 = |\Sigma V^T \mathbf{w}|^2$ (using the fact that $U$ is orthonormal and preserves norms), set $\mathbf{v} = V^T\mathbf{w}$. The problem becomes minimizing $|\Sigma \mathbf{v}|^2$ subject to $|\mathbf{v}|^2 = 1$. The diagonal matrix $\Sigma$ scales each component of $\mathbf{v}$ by the corresponding singular value $\sigma_i$. To minimize the result, point $\mathbf{v}$ entirely in the direction of the smallest singular value — i.e., $\mathbf{v} = [0, 1]^T$ (the last standard basis vector, since singular values are sorted in descending order). Recovering $\mathbf{w} = V\mathbf{v}$ gives: the optimal line normal is the last column of $V$ in the SVD of the centered data matrix. This elegant result says that total least squares finds the direction of minimum variance in the data — the direction along which the data varies least, which is perpendicular to the best-fit line. This SVD interpretation has a beautiful geometric meaning: SVD finds the principal axes of the data cloud, and total least squares picks the axis of least spread as the line normal. An outlier is a data point that lies far from the true structure — perhaps due to a sensor glitch, a misidentified feature match, or a measurement from a completely different structure in the scene. A natural response is to use a robust cost function that grows more slowly for large residuals. When $u_i$ is large (outlier), $C \to 1$ — the cost saturates, capping the damage any single outlier can do. The parameter $\sigma$ — the scale parameter — controls the transition between “treated as inlier” and “treated as outlier.” A large $\sigma$ behaves nearly like standard least squares. A small $\sigma$ treats almost everything as an outlier and fits only the very closest points. Choosing $\sigma$ well is essential but non-trivial; it typically requires some knowledge of the noise scale. Because robust cost functions are nonlinear, they cannot be minimized in closed form. Instead, the standard approach is to start with the least-squares solution as initialization, then iteratively minimize the robust objective using gradient-based methods until convergence. Part 2: RANSAC — Robust Fitting Through Random Sampling A Different Philosophy Entirely Robust cost functions approach the outlier problem by down-weighting suspicious points. RANSAC — RAndom SAmple Consensus — takes a completely different approach: rather than trying to fit all the data while mitigating outlier influence, it finds the subset of the data that is most consistent with some model and fits only that subset. The Algorithm RANSAC for line fitting works as follows. Suppose we have $N$ points that we believe mostly lie along a single line, with some outliers scattered randomly. Step 1 — Sample: Randomly choose the minimum number of points needed to define the model. For a line, this is exactly 2 points. (For a homography, it would be 4 point correspondences. For a fundamental matrix, it would be 8.) Step 2 — Fit: Fit the model to the sampled points. For two points, there is exactly one line through them. Step 3 — Evaluate: Count the inliers — all data points within a distance threshold $\delta$ of the fitted model. Formally, the inlier set is: \(P = \{(x_i, y_i) \mid r((x_i, y_i), \mathbf{w}) < \delta\}\) where $r$ is the residual (perpendicular distance to the line) and $\delta$ is a pre-chosen tolerance. The outlier set is simply everything not in $P$. Step 4 — Repeat: Go back to Step 1 with a new random sample. Do this for $n$ iterations. Rather than trying to extract a story that reconciles every account (including the unreliable ones), the detective finds the largest group of witnesses whose stories are mutually consistent, and builds the case from those. If 50% of your data are outliers ($\epsilon = 0.5$), fitting a line ($s = 2$), and you want 99% confidence ($p = 0.99$): \[n = \frac{\log(0.01)}{\log(1 - 0.25)} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.288} \approx 16\] Just 16 iterations are sufficient! RANSAC is remarkably efficient because even with many outliers, the probability of drawing a clean small sample in repeated trials grows quickly. The formula also reveals when RANSAC becomes expensive: when the model requires a large minimum sample size $s$, or when the outlier fraction $\epsilon$ is very high, the required $n$ grows rapidly. What Makes RANSAC Special RANSAC has a combination of properties that make it uniquely suited to computer vision: It is general — the same algorithm structure applies to any parametric model. Change the sampling step and the fitting step, and you have RANSAC for homographies, fundamental matrices, circles, planes, or any other geometric model. In practice, RANSAC is the standard preprocessing step before computing homographies or fundamental matrices from feature point matches, precisely because the matches always contain false matches (outliers) that would corrupt standard least squares. It is interpretable — after running RANSAC, you have an explicit inlier set and an explicit outlier set. You know which points the algorithm believes are consistent with the model, and which are not. This transparency is valuable in debugging and analysis. It is robust to high outlier rates — as long as there is a sufficiently large inlier set, RANSAC will find it even when outliers dominate the data. The main limitations are that $\delta$ (the inlier threshold) and $n$ (the iteration count) need to be specified, RANSAC is probabilistic (there is always a small chance of failure), and when outlier rates are extreme (above roughly 80-90%), the required iteration count explodes. Part 3: The Hough Transform — Voting in Parameter Space A Completely Different Way of Thinking About Fitting Both least squares and RANSAC work by proposing a model and checking how many points agree with it. The Hough transform takes yet another approach — it is fundamentally a voting procedure, and it expresses a profound duality between image space and parameter space. The core insight is this: rather than asking “what line fits these points?”, flip the question around and ask “what lines are consistent with each individual point?” Each point has an opinion about all possible lines that could pass through it. If you let every point vote for all lines it is consistent with, then the line that the most points agree on will accumulate the most votes. That line is your answer. The Image-to-Parameter Duality Let us make this precise for lines of the form $y = mx + n$ (using $n$ for the intercept to avoid confusion with the iteration count). A single point $(x_i, y_i)$ in image space lies on every line $y = mx + n$ satisfying $y_i = m x_i + n$, or equivalently: \[n = -x_i m + y_i\] This is a line in parameter space $(m, n)$ — a linear relationship between the possible slope $m$ and intercept $n$ values. Every $(m, n)$ pair on this line in parameter space corresponds to a line $y = mx + n$ in image space that passes through $(x_i, y_i)$. Now consider two image points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$. Each maps to a line in parameter space. If these two points lie on the same image line with parameters $(m’, n’)$, then both parameter-space lines pass through the same point $(m’, n’)$. In other words, the two lines in parameter space intersect at the parameters of the true fitting line. This is the central magic of the Hough transform: collinear points in image space become concurrent lines in parameter space. Finding a line that fits many points is equivalent to finding a point in parameter space where many lines intersect — a peak in a 2D accumulator. The Practical Algorithm In practice, the Hough voting procedure works as follows: Divide the parameter space into a discrete grid of cells, each cell corresponding to a range of $(m, n)$ values. Initialize all cell counts to zero. For each data point $(x_i, y_i)$, compute all parameter-space cells $(m, n)$ that satisfy $n = -x_im + y_i$ (approximately, snapping to the nearest grid cell), and increment each such cell by 1. After processing all data points, find the cell with the highest count. The corresponding $(m, n)$ values are the parameters of the best-fit line. Each point contributes at most one vote per candidate line — hence the “voting” interpretation. Points that lie near a true line will vote heavily for the corresponding parameter-space cell. Random outliers will spread their votes diffusely across many cells, never concentrating enough to form a peak. One attractive property of the Hough transform is that it naturally handles multiple structures in the data. If the scene contains two lines, there will be two peaks in parameter space. Each peak corresponds to one line, and the votes for each peak come from the points on that line. This is something standard least squares fundamentally cannot do — it fits a single model to everything. RANSAC can handle multiple structures by running sequentially (fit one model, remove its inliers, repeat), but the Hough transform detects all of them simultaneously. The Problem with Slope-Intercept Parameters: Unbounded Space There is a significant practical problem with using $(m, n)$ as the parameter space: the slope $m$ is unbounded. A nearly vertical line has $m \to \pm\infty$, making it impossible to allocate a finite grid. This is the same problem we encountered with ordinary least squares. The solution is to switch to the polar parameterization of lines: \[x\cos(\theta) + y\sin(\theta) = \rho\] In this representation: $\rho$ is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line — bounded by the maximum distance between any two points in the dataset, which for an image of width $W$ and height $H$ is at most $\sqrt{W^2 + H^2}$. $\theta$ is the angle of the line’s normal vector with respect to the $x$-axis — bounded in $[0, \pi)$. Both parameters are finite, so the parameter space grid is finite. Every line, regardless of orientation, is representable. With the polar parameterization, a single image point $(x_i, y_i)$ corresponds not to a straight line in parameter space, but to a sinusoidal curve: \[\rho = x_i \cos(\theta) + y_i \sin(\theta)\] For different values of $\theta$, this traces out a sinusoid in the $(\theta, \rho)$ plane. Collinear image points produce sinusoids that all pass through the same $(\theta, \rho)$ point — the intersection corresponds to the parameters of the common line. The voting procedure is otherwise identical: for each data point, trace the sinusoid in the $(\theta, \rho)$ grid and increment all touched cells; after processing all points, find the peak. Handling Noise and Choosing Grid Resolution A key practical parameter in the Hough transform is the grid cell size $w$. Noisy data points that theoretically should lie on the same line will, in practice, trace sinusoids that do not intersect at exactly one point but rather form a small cluster of nearby intersections. A grid cell that is too fine will have these votes scattered across several cells, producing no clear peak. A coarser grid bins these nearby votes together, producing a clean peak. But coarser grids introduce their own problem: cells that are too large will merge the votes of two genuinely different nearby lines, blurring them into a single broad peak and losing the ability to distinguish the lines. This is the classical resolution-precision trade-off: fine grids give precise answers but are sensitive to noise; coarse grids tolerate noise but lose precision. In the presence of truly uniform noise — points scattered randomly everywhere with no underlying structure — the Hough space will be covered with spurious peaks of roughly equal height, and no single candidate line will achieve a decisive majority. The Hough transform, like all fitting methods, requires that the signal-to-noise ratio be sufficient for the structure to be detectable. Putting It All Together: When to Use Which Method These three fitting strategies are not competing alternatives — they are complementary tools, each suited to different conditions. Ordinary least squares is the right starting point when your data is relatively clean and you have a direct, linear parameterization of the model. It is fast, produces a unique solution, and has a beautiful closed-form expression. It is the backbone of camera calibration, homography computation, and fundamental matrix estimation — but always in combination with a robustification step. Total least squares with SVD is needed when the error should be measured symmetrically (e.g., fitting lines, planes, or subspaces), or whenever the minimum-norm solution to an underdetermined system is needed. The SVD solution appears throughout computer vision: PCA for dimensionality reduction, the eight-point algorithm for the fundamental matrix, the DLT algorithm for homographies. Understanding total least squares via SVD is understanding the backbone of geometric fitting. RANSAC is the right tool when the data contains a significant fraction of gross outliers that least squares cannot handle — which is nearly always the case in practical feature matching across images. Standard practice in image stitching, visual odometry, and 3D reconstruction is to use RANSAC to find a clean inlier set, then apply least squares to that inlier set for the final parameter estimate. The combination is highly robust and broadly applicable. The Hough transform shines when you want to detect multiple structures simultaneously without committing to how many there are, when the data might not be organized into explicit correspondences, or when you want a method that is inherently tolerant of missing data and partial occlusion. It is particularly powerful for detecting lines in edge images (as in lane detection), circles (as in iris detection), and any shape that can be parameterized compactly. Its main cost is memory and computation for the parameter space accumulator. Conclusion: The Art and Mathematics of Model Fitting The progression from least squares to RANSAC to the Hough transform tells a coherent story about how algorithms can be made more and more robust to the messiness of real data. Least squares is optimal when the world cooperates — when noise is small, Gaussian, and free of outliers. It is the right answer to the question “what if all my data is trustworthy?” The mathematics is elegant: the normal equations, the pseudoinverse, SVD — a toolkit of remarkable power and generality that extends far beyond line fitting to virtually every parametric model in computer vision. Robust cost functions acknowledge that the world does not always cooperate, and try to give outliers less influence without discarding them. They are a continuous, gradient-friendly compromise between trusting all data and ignoring suspicious data. RANSAC takes the more aggressive stance of deciding which data to trust, based on consensus. By repeatedly hypothesizing a model from a tiny random sample and asking how many points agree, it navigates the chicken-and-egg problem of needing good data to find the model and needing the model to identify good data. The probabilistic analysis gives a clear, principled way to choose how many iterations are enough. The Hough transform reframes the fitting problem entirely. Instead of asking “what model fits the data?” it asks each data point “what models are you consistent with?” and aggregates the answers. The duality between image space and parameter space — points become lines, lines become points — is one of the most elegant ideas in classical computer vision, and the extension to polar coordinates makes it a practical workhorse for line and shape detection. Mastering these methods is not just about knowing their formulas. It is about developing the intuition for why each one is designed the way it is — what failure mode in the previous method each new technique was designed to overcome, and what assumptions each one relies on. That design intuition is what allows you to choose the right tool for the problem at hand, and to adapt these classical methods to new challenges as they arise. This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 6: Fitting and Matching, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

entry.title: Monocular Depth Estimation and Feature Tracking

link.title: Monocular Depth Estimation and Feature Tracking

entry.content:
Teaching Machines to See Depth: Monocular Depth Estimation and Feature Tracking

How modern computer vision systems learn to recover 3D structure from flat images — without lasers, without stereo cameras, and sometimes without any human labels at all.

Close your right eye and look around the room. You can still judge distances. You can tell which chair is closer, which wall is farther, roughly how far away your coffee cup is. Your brain is performing a remarkable computational feat: inferring a three-dimensional world from a two-dimensional retinal image, using nothing but subtle visual cues baked into a single photograph of reality.


For decades, computer vision researchers assumed this was essentially impossible to automate reliably. Depth, they argued, is fundamentally lost when a 3D scene is projected onto a 2D sensor — the math is irreversible. And in a strict geometric sense, they were right. But as this article will show, geometry is not the only source of depth information. Texture gradients, occlusion patterns, lighting, shadows, and the statistical regularities of natural scenes all carry depth signals that a sufficiently powerful learning system can exploit.

This article explores two closely related problems that sit at the heart of modern computer vision: monocular depth estimation (recovering depth from a single image) and feature tracking (consistently identifying the same physical points across a sequence of images). Both problems, at their core, are instances of the same fundamental challenge — the correspondence problem — and modern deep learning has transformed how we attack both. We’ll trace the intellectual journey from geometric first principles through supervised learning to the elegant self-supervised approaches that have pushed the state of the art, and we’ll examine the loss functions, architectures, and training tricks that make it all work.

The Correspondence Problem: The Thread Connecting Everything

Before diving into depth estimation specifically, it’s worth understanding the underlying problem that unifies much of geometric computer vision. The correspondence problem asks: given two or more images of the same scene, which pixel in image A corresponds to which pixel in image B?

This seems simple at first — just find the same point in both images. But in practice it is extraordinarily difficult. Lighting changes between images. Objects may be partially occluded. Regions of uniform texture (a white wall, a clear sky) offer no distinguishing information. Repetitive patterns (a brick facade, a tiled floor) create ambiguous matches. And at the scale of a full image with millions of pixels, brute-force search is computationally intractable.


Both depth estimation and feature tracking are essentially specialized versions of solving this correspondence problem. For depth estimation, we want to find correspondences between a left camera image and a right camera image (or between frames in a video) so we can triangulate to recover 3D position. For feature tracking, we want to find correspondences for specific interesting points across many frames of video. The same techniques, the same mathematical tools, and — increasingly — the same deep learning architectures apply to both.

Part One: Monocular Depth Estimation

Why Depth Matters, and Why It’s Hard

Depth perception is a prerequisite for almost every meaningful interaction with the physical world. A robot arm reaching for an object needs to know how far away it is. An autonomous vehicle needs to know whether the pedestrian ahead is 5 meters away or 50. A 3D reconstruction pipeline needs per-pixel depth to build a model of a scene. Augmented reality systems need depth to occlude virtual objects correctly with real ones.

Active depth sensors like LiDAR (which fires laser pulses and measures return times) and structured light systems (which project known patterns and observe their deformation) solve this problem directly and accurately. But they are expensive, power-hungry, mechanically complex, and can struggle in bright outdoor environments where the ambient light washes out the sensor’s signal. A camera, by contrast, is cheap, passive, lightweight, and works anywhere.

The question is whether the information latent in a photograph is sufficient to recover depth — and, increasingly, the answer from deep learning is yes.

The Geometry of Stereo: Building Intuition for Depth from Disparity

To understand why depth estimation works at all, we need to first understand the stereo geometry that underlies it — even when we eventually move to a monocular (single-camera) setup.

Imagine two cameras mounted side by side, their optical axes pointing in the same direction, separated by a horizontal distance $b$ called the baseline. This is exactly how your two eyes are arranged. When both cameras observe the same 3D point $P$, that point appears at slightly different horizontal positions in the two images. The farther away $P$ is, the smaller this horizontal shift. The closer it is, the larger the shift. This horizontal shift is called disparity, and it is the key to recovering depth.

To make this precise, consider the setup with the two camera image planes aligned (a configuration called rectified stereo). In this case, corresponding points in the two images lie on the same horizontal scan line — a constraint known as the epipolar constraint. The disparity $d$ between corresponding points $p$ (in the left image) and $p’$ (in the right image) is simply:

\[d = p'_u - p_u\]

where $p_u$ and $p’_u$ are the horizontal pixel coordinates in the left and right images respectively. By similar triangles relating the camera geometry, the depth $z$ of the point (its distance along the optical axis) is:

\[z = \frac{f \cdot b}{d} \tag{1}\]

Here, $f$ is the focal length of the cameras and $b$ is the baseline length. The relationship is elegantly simple and deeply intuitive: depth is inversely proportional to disparity. A point very far away produces nearly identical images in both cameras (small disparity, large depth). A point right in front of the cameras looks very different in the two views (large disparity, small depth).

This formula reveals something important: to recover depth, all we need to do is find correspondences between the two images. If we can identify which pixel in the right image corresponds to each pixel in the left image, we know the disparity everywhere, and therefore the depth everywhere. The depth estimation problem reduces to the correspondence problem.
