Deeper layers responded to object parts — eyes, wheels, faces — and the deepest layers responded to entire objects.

This convergence suggests that the hierarchical structure of good representations is not just a human design preference — it is, in some sense, the correct structure for visual understanding, one that learning discovers on its own when given enough data and capacity. The hand-crafted pipelines were approximating the right answer; the learned ones found it more precisely.


Visualizing the Learned Space with t-SNE

Another window into learned representations is dimensionality reduction. The intermediate representation of a trained neural network is a high-dimensional vector (perhaps 2048 dimensions for a modern ResNet). We can’t directly visualize 2048 dimensions, but we can project them down to 2D for inspection using t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embeddings).

t-SNE works by minimizing the KL divergence between a probability distribution over pairs of points in high-dimensional space (where “probability” reflects similarity — nearby points have high probability) and the corresponding distribution in 2D space. The result is a 2D map where nearby points in the original high-dimensional representation end up nearby in the 2D visualization.

When applied to the intermediate representations of a well-trained CNN, the t-SNE plot reveals that images of the same class cluster together, even across considerable visual variation. Images of the digit “3” from MNIST, written in many different handwriting styles, all land in the same region of the 2D map. This is powerful evidence that the learned representation has captured something genuinely semantic — “three-ness” — rather than superficial pixel statistics. The representation has disentangled the identity of the digit from the style of its rendering.


Part 6: Learning Without Labels — Autoencoders and Self-Supervised Learning

The Label Bottleneck

Supervised learning requires labeled data. For image classification, every training image needs a class label. For pose estimation, every training image needs a 6D pose annotation. For object detection, every image needs bounding boxes. Acquiring these labels is expensive: it requires human annotators, domain expertise, and time. A medical dataset might require a specialist to label each image; a robotics dataset might require expensive motion-capture equipment.

Meanwhile, unlabeled data is essentially free. Every camera ever deployed generates a continuous stream of images. Every robot generates a continuous stream of sensor readings. The question becomes: can we learn meaningful representations from this ocean of unlabeled data?

The answer, developed over the past decade and now central to modern AI, is yes.

The Autoencoder: Learning by Compression

The autoencoder is the foundational idea for unsupervised representation learning. Its architecture is symmetric: an encoder network compresses the input $\mathbf{X}$ (say, an image) into a low-dimensional intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$, and a decoder network attempts to reconstruct the original input from $\mathbf{z}$, producing $\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{X})$.

The training objective is simply to minimize the reconstruction loss — the difference between the input and its reconstruction:

\[\arg\min_{\mathcal{F}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}} \left[ \| \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{X}) - \mathbf{X} \| \right]\]


No external labels are needed. The input image itself serves as the training target.

The magic lies in the bottleneck. The intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$ has far fewer dimensions than the input $\mathbf{X}$. To successfully reconstruct $\mathbf{X}$ from $\mathbf{z}$, the encoder must learn to compress the most important information about $\mathbf{X}$ into those few dimensions. Redundant information (background noise, uninformative correlations) gets discarded; the information that distinguishes one input from another must be preserved. This is exactly the kind of compact, explanatory representation we want.

Concretely: if you train an autoencoder on a dataset of face images, the bottleneck representation $\mathbf{z}$ will likely encode attributes like identity, expression, pose, and lighting — because these are the factors that vary across faces and that the decoder needs in order to reconstruct the image. Factors that are constant across all images (like “has two eyes and a nose”) don’t need to be in $\mathbf{z}$ because the decoder can learn them as default assumptions.

The encoder half of a trained autoencoder is a powerful, general-purpose feature extractor. It can be applied to new images to produce compact representations, which can then be used as inputs to downstream classifiers or other models. And it was trained entirely without labels.

Self-Supervised Learning: Creating Your Own Labels

Self-supervised learning extends this idea further by creating synthetic training targets from the data itself, without any human annotation. The key move is to deliberately withhold part of the input and ask the model to predict the missing part.

In one simple example, take an image, hide the upper half, and ask the network to reconstruct the upper half given the lower half. The lower triangle of pixels is the input; the upper triangle is the label — generated automatically from the same image. No human annotation required.

The intuition is that to successfully predict the missing region, the network must understand the semantic content of the image at some level. A model that has truly understood “this is a fish swimming near coral” can make a reasonable prediction about what the top of the image looks like, even though it hasn’t seen it. A model that has memorized pixel statistics without understanding content cannot.


This idea, seemingly simple, has produced some of the most powerful models in modern AI. The BERT family of language models is trained by masking random words and predicting them from context. The MAE (Masked Autoencoder) for images masks large random patches of an image and trains the model to reconstruct them. These self-supervised objectives, applied at scale, produce representations that transfer remarkably well to downstream tasks — often matching or exceeding the performance of supervised methods trained on large labeled datasets.

The Transfer Learning Payoff

What makes unsupervised and self-supervised pre-training so valuable in practice is the concept of transfer learning. The workflow proceeds in two stages:

First, train the encoder (or the full self-supervised model) on a large unlabeled dataset. This pre-training phase is computationally expensive but can be done once and the result shared broadly. The model learns a rich, general-purpose intermediate representation.

Second, for a specific downstream task (say, medical image classification), collect a small labeled dataset — perhaps a few thousand examples, which is far cheaper to annotate than millions. Train a lightweight classifier on top of the frozen (or lightly fine-tuned) encoder. Because the encoder has already learned to produce meaningful, compact representations, the classifier needs very little data to achieve high accuracy.


This two-stage approach has become the dominant paradigm in modern AI. The large-scale pre-training provides the “representational foundation,” and the small labeled dataset provides the task-specific “finishing touches.” It is representation learning in its most practically powerful form.

Conclusion: The Representation Is the Intelligence

Looking across the full arc of this essay — from walking robots and Markov chains, through the hand-crafted features of classical computer vision, to learned representations and self-supervised autoencoders — a unifying theme emerges. The way you represent information is not a minor implementation detail. It is, in a deep sense, the intelligence itself.

A perfect state representation that satisfies the Markov property allows simple dynamics models to make accurate predictions. A compact, disentangled intermediate representation allows a simple classifier to generalize robustly. A rich, hierarchical learned representation allows a model trained on one task to transfer to another with minimal additional data. In each case, the quality of the representation determines the ceiling on what the downstream system can achieve.

The evolution from hand-crafted to learned representations is not the story of humans becoming unnecessary — it is the story of human insight being applied at a higher level of abstraction. Rather than designing features, we now design learning objectives (reconstruction loss, mask prediction, contrastive similarity), architectures (convolutional networks, transformers), and training regimes. The features emerge automatically, and they turn out to be better than what we could have designed by hand — because the data contains patterns that our intuitions don’t anticipate.

The question “what is the right representation?” remains as central and difficult as ever. But we now have powerful tools for answering it empirically — by training, evaluating, visualizing, and iterating. Understanding these tools, and the conceptual framework that connects states, observations, generative models, and learned features, is the foundation for everything that follows in modern robotics and computer vision.

This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 7: Representations and Representation Learning, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

The dynamics function $f(\cdot)$ can be nonlinear and complex, but the structure is the same: the present state determines the next state. The Markov Property — Why the Present Is Enough There is a crucial simplifying assumption that underlies most of the mathematical machinery in this space: the Markov property. It states that the future depends only on the present, not on how we got here. Formally: \[P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t, x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_2, x_1) = P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t)\] This is a profound claim. It says that once you know the current state $x_t$, the entire history $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{t-1}$ becomes irrelevant for predicting $x_{t+1}$. The state “summarizes” all the past information that matters for the future. Is the Markov property always true in practice? Not necessarily — a robot’s current joint angle might not tell you everything about its trajectory if there’s unmodeled history (like accumulated fatigue or temperature effects). But it is a tremendously useful approximation, and choosing a state representation that makes the Markov property approximately true is itself part of good state design. A system that includes both position and velocity is more likely to be Markovian than one that tracks only position, since knowing “where I am and how fast I’m moving” is usually sufficient to predict “where I’ll be next.” Systems that evolve with the Markov property are called Markov chains, and they are visualized as a sequence of state nodes where each node depends only on its immediate predecessor — a clean chain of causal influence through time. When the State Is Hidden: Observations and Estimation Markov chains assume we can directly observe the state $x_t$ at each timestep. But in practice, this is rarely true. A robot doesn’t “know” its joint angles — it reads them from noisy sensors. A self-driving car doesn’t directly perceive the 3D positions and velocities of surrounding vehicles — it receives raw camera frames and LiDAR point clouds and must infer those quantities. This is the problem of state estimation: recovering the true (hidden) state from noisy, indirect observations. The appropriate model is the Hidden Markov Model (HMM), which adds an observation layer on top of the Markov chain. The states $x_t$ evolve as a Markov process, but we only see observations $z_t$ (sensor readings, images, etc.), where each observation depends only on the current state: \[P(z_t \mid x_t, x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_1) = P(z_t \mid x_t)\] The function $h(x_t) = z_t$ is called the observation model — it describes how the hidden state generates what we actually measure. For a camera on a self-driving car, $h$ is essentially the projection function mapping 3D world positions to 2D image pixels. This two-layer structure — hidden states evolving according to dynamics, observed through a noisy sensor model — is one of the most widely applicable models in all of engineering. From GPS-aided navigation to speech recognition to visual tracking, HMMs and their extensions appear everywhere. Adding Actions: The Full Decision-Making Picture The HMM framework becomes even richer when we add a third element: control inputs. Instead of the dynamics being $f(x_t) = x_{t+1}$, we have $f(x_t, u_t) = x_{t+1}$, where $u_t$ is the action taken by the agent at time $t$. For the walking robot, $u_t$ might be the torque commands sent to each joint motor. For the self-driving car, it might be steering angle and throttle. This extension transforms the Markov chain into a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and the HMM into a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP). The central question of these frameworks is no longer just “what is the current state?” but “what action should I take?” — the problem of decision-making under uncertainty. This is the foundation of reinforcement learning and optimal control, though exploring those areas fully is a separate journey. Part 2: Generative vs. Discriminative Approaches to State Estimation Two Fundamentally Different Philosophies Once we have the HMM framework in hand — states, observations, dynamics, and observation models — the question becomes practical: given an observation $z$ (say, a camera image), how do we estimate the state $x$ (say, the 6D pose of an object in the scene)? There are two philosophically distinct approaches, and understanding their difference is essential to understanding modern machine learning. A generative model asks: what joint probability distribution $p(z, x)$ describes how observations and states co-occur? To use Bayes’ rule, this factors as $p(z, x) = p(z \mid x) \cdot p(x)$, where $p(z \mid x)$ is the observation likelihood (how likely is this image given this pose?) and $p(x)$ is a prior over states (how likely is this pose in the first place?). To estimate the pose from an image, you can sample candidate poses from the prior, use the observation model to “render” what the scene would look like in each pose, and find the candidate that best matches the actual image. The generative model is modeling the process by which observations are created. A discriminative model takes a more direct approach. Instead of modeling how the world generates observations, it directly models the conditional probability $p(x \mid z)$ — given this observation, what is the state? You train a function (nowadays almost always a neural network) to map directly from input image to output pose. PoseCNN, for instance, takes an RGB image as input and outputs semantic labels, 3D translation estimates, and 3D rotation estimates simultaneously. The discriminative model doesn’t need to know how images are generated — it just needs to learn the mapping from image to answer. The tradeoff is a classic one in machine learning. Generative models are more interpretable and can leverage physical knowledge (e.g., the laws of optics tell us how a 3D object projects onto a 2D image). They can also generate new data and handle missing information more gracefully. Discriminative models tend to be more accurate on their target task when trained on sufficient data, because they don’t waste capacity modeling aspects of the world irrelevant to the prediction — but they can be black boxes, and they typically require labeled data. Part 3: What Is a Representation, Really? The Three Layers of a Computer Vision Pipeline Now we turn to a more specific and modern question: in the context of computer vision and machine learning, what exactly do we mean by a “representation,” and why does it matter so much? Consider a complete vision pipeline. On one end, you have raw sensor data — a $1920 \times 1080$ RGB image, a depth map, a LiDAR point cloud. This is the input representation: the format in which raw perceptual data arrives. On the other end, you have whatever the system needs to produce — a class label (“fish”), a bounding box, a 6D pose, a segmentation mask. This is the output representation: a compact, task-specific summary of what matters for downstream decision-making. In between these two ends sits the most interesting layer: the intermediate representation. This is a compressed, low-dimensional encoding of the high-dimensional input that captures the information necessary to derive the output. In a deep neural network, the intermediate representation is the activation vector at some internal layer — a dense numerical vector, perhaps of dimension 512 or 2048, that summarizes the content of the input image in a form the output layer can use. The intermediate representation is where most of the intellectual action happens in modern computer vision, because it is here that raw pixels are transformed into something semantically meaningful. How this transformation happens — whether by hand or by learning — is the central story of the last decade of computer vision research. What Makes a Good Representation? This is not just a practical question but a theoretical one, and Yoshua Bengio and colleagues have articulated a set of properties that a good representation should ideally satisfy. A good representation should be compact: it should use as few dimensions as possible. A $1920 \times 1080$ RGB image contains roughly 6 million numbers. Most of those numbers are redundant — neighboring pixels are correlated, the background is uninformative, the color distribution is constrained. A compact representation discards this redundancy and retains only what matters. At the same time, it must be explanatory — expressive enough to capture the full range of relevant variation in the input. A representation that collapses all images to a single number is perfectly compact but useless. The tension between compactness and expressiveness is the fundamental challenge of representation design. A good representation should also be disentangled. This means that different factors of variation in the world — an object’s shape, its color, its position, the lighting — should be encoded in different, independent parts of the representation. If you change the lighting in a scene, a disentangled representation should change only in the “lighting” dimensions, leaving the “object identity” dimensions unchanged. Disentanglement makes representations more generalizable, more interpretable, and more useful for downstream tasks that may care about only some factors. The property of being hierarchical reflects the observation that the world has structure at multiple scales. Edges compose into textures, textures into parts, parts into objects, objects into scenes. A good representation captures this hierarchy, allowing low-level features to be reused in the construction of high-level concepts — much as the same edge detector is useful for recognizing both dogs and cars, even though those are very different categories. Finally, and most pragmatically, a good representation should make downstream tasks easier. This is ultimately the ground truth criterion: does using this representation improve the accuracy, efficiency, or robustness of the classification, detection, or control system that consumes it? The quality of a representation can always be measured, at least indirectly, by the downstream performance it enables. Part 4: Hand-Crafted Representations — The Classical Era The Philosophy of Feature Engineering For most of the history of computer vision (roughly up to 2012), intermediate representations were designed by humans. The process was called feature engineering or feature extraction, and it occupied a large fraction of the field’s intellectual energy. The philosophy was intuitive: if you want to recognize a clownfish, you reason about what makes a clownfish visually distinctive — its orange and white stripes, its particular body shape, its characteristic fin structure. You then design mathematical operations on the image that detect these properties: edge detectors to find stripe boundaries, color histograms to capture the orange-white distribution, texture descriptors to characterize surface patterns. The result is a vector of numbers — a feature descriptor — that encodes these human-defined properties. This hand-crafted intermediate representation is then fed into a classifier (a support vector machine, a decision tree, or a simple neural network) that learns to map from the feature vector to a class label. The two stages — feature extraction and classification — were largely separate. The pipeline had a natural hierarchical structure. Low-level features (raw edges, color gradients) were combined into mid-level features (segments, textures), which were combined into high-level features (parts, body plan), which were used to make the final prediction. This mirrors the way humans describe visual objects: a clownfish has fins (part), which have stripes (texture), which have sharp color boundaries (edges). The Strengths and Limits of Hand-Crafted Features The primary virtue of hand-crafted representations is interpretability. Because a human designed every feature, a human can explain why it matters. If a classifier rejects an image as “not a clownfish,” you can trace back through the features and understand what was missing — perhaps the color histogram didn’t have enough orange, or the edge detector didn’t find the expected stripe pattern. In high-stakes domains — medical imaging, legal evidence analysis, safety-critical robotics — this transparency can be essential. The limitations, however, are severe. Designing good features requires deep domain expertise. It is slow, laborious, and often produces features that are brittle: they work well in the conditions for which they were designed but fail when the lighting changes, the viewing angle shifts, or the object is partially occluded. And crucially, the features are designed to capture what humans think is relevant, which may not align with what is actually most predictive. For tasks where human intuition is a good guide, hand-crafted features work surprisingly well. For tasks where the relevant patterns are subtle, high-dimensional, or not easily articulable in human terms — like distinguishing malignant from benign tissue in a histology slide, or estimating the emotional state of a pedestrian from their gait — hand-crafted features simply can’t compete. Part 5: Learned Representations — The Modern Era The Neural Network Revolution Around 2012, a shift occurred that is now widely recognized as one of the most dramatic transitions in the history of machine learning. Driven by the combination of large labeled datasets (like ImageNet, with over a million labeled images), cheap parallel computation (GPUs), and algorithmic improvements to deep neural networks — most importantly, the systematic training of deep convolutional architectures — learned representations displaced hand-crafted ones as the dominant paradigm in computer vision. The key idea is simple to state but profound in its implications: instead of designing the intermediate representation by hand, you train a neural network end-to-end, and let the learning process discover the representation automatically. The convolutional layers of the network learn to act as feature extractors — but the features they learn are optimized for the task at hand, not for what a human engineer thought was important. The result, empirically, was a dramatic improvement in accuracy across nearly every vision benchmark. Networks trained on ImageNet achieved error rates that human-engineered systems could not approach. What Do Neural Networks Actually Learn? This success raises an immediate question: what, exactly, are the learned features? They are not designed to be interpretable, and the activations of internal layers are just large vectors of numbers. Can we understand them? Zeiler and Fergus, in a landmark 2014 paper, visualized the learned representations of a deep CNN trained on ImageNet by finding the input image patches that maximally activated each filter at each layer. Their discovery was striking and somewhat surprising: the learned representations were hierarchical in the same way as the hand-crafted ones. Early layers in the network responded to simple edges and color gradients. Middle layers responded to textures and patterns. Deeper layers responded to object parts — eyes, wheels, faces — and the deepest layers responded to entire objects. This convergence suggests that the hierarchical structure of good representations is not just a human design preference — it is, in some sense, the correct structure for visual understanding, one that learning discovers on its own when given enough data and capacity. The hand-crafted pipelines were approximating the right answer; the learned ones found it more precisely. Visualizing the Learned Space with t-SNE Another window into learned representations is dimensionality reduction. The intermediate representation of a trained neural network is a high-dimensional vector (perhaps 2048 dimensions for a modern ResNet). We can’t directly visualize 2048 dimensions, but we can project them down to 2D for inspection using t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embeddings). t-SNE works by minimizing the KL divergence between a probability distribution over pairs of points in high-dimensional space (where “probability” reflects similarity — nearby points have high probability) and the corresponding distribution in 2D space. The result is a 2D map where nearby points in the original high-dimensional representation end up nearby in the 2D visualization. When applied to the intermediate representations of a well-trained CNN, the t-SNE plot reveals that images of the same class cluster together, even across considerable visual variation. Images of the digit “3” from MNIST, written in many different handwriting styles, all land in the same region of the 2D map. This is powerful evidence that the learned representation has captured something genuinely semantic — “three-ness” — rather than superficial pixel statistics. The representation has disentangled the identity of the digit from the style of its rendering. Part 6: Learning Without Labels — Autoencoders and Self-Supervised Learning The Label Bottleneck Supervised learning requires labeled data. For image classification, every training image needs a class label. For pose estimation, every training image needs a 6D pose annotation. For object detection, every image needs bounding boxes. Acquiring these labels is expensive: it requires human annotators, domain expertise, and time. A medical dataset might require a specialist to label each image; a robotics dataset might require expensive motion-capture equipment. Meanwhile, unlabeled data is essentially free. Every camera ever deployed generates a continuous stream of images. Every robot generates a continuous stream of sensor readings. The question becomes: can we learn meaningful representations from this ocean of unlabeled data? The answer, developed over the past decade and now central to modern AI, is yes. The Autoencoder: Learning by Compression The autoencoder is the foundational idea for unsupervised representation learning. Its architecture is symmetric: an encoder network compresses the input $\mathbf{X}$ (say, an image) into a low-dimensional intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$, and a decoder network attempts to reconstruct the original input from $\mathbf{z}$, producing $\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{X})$. The training objective is simply to minimize the reconstruction loss — the difference between the input and its reconstruction: \[\arg\min_{\mathcal{F}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}} \left[ \| \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{X}) - \mathbf{X} \| \right]\] No external labels are needed. The input image itself serves as the training target. The magic lies in the bottleneck. The intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$ has far fewer dimensions than the input $\mathbf{X}$. To successfully reconstruct $\mathbf{X}$ from $\mathbf{z}$, the encoder must learn to compress the most important information about $\mathbf{X}$ into those few dimensions. Redundant information (background noise, uninformative correlations) gets discarded; the information that distinguishes one input from another must be preserved. This is exactly the kind of compact, explanatory representation we want. Concretely: if you train an autoencoder on a dataset of face images, the bottleneck representation $\mathbf{z}$ will likely encode attributes like identity, expression, pose, and lighting — because these are the factors that vary across faces and that the decoder needs in order to reconstruct the image. Factors that are constant across all images (like “has two eyes and a nose”) don’t need to be in $\mathbf{z}$ because the decoder can learn them as default assumptions. The encoder half of a trained autoencoder is a powerful, general-purpose feature extractor. It can be applied to new images to produce compact representations, which can then be used as inputs to downstream classifiers or other models. And it was trained entirely without labels. Self-Supervised Learning: Creating Your Own Labels Self-supervised learning extends this idea further by creating synthetic training targets from the data itself, without any human annotation. The key move is to deliberately withhold part of the input and ask the model to predict the missing part. In one simple example, take an image, hide the upper half, and ask the network to reconstruct the upper half given the lower half. The lower triangle of pixels is the input; the upper triangle is the label — generated automatically from the same image. No human annotation required. The intuition is that to successfully predict the missing region, the network must understand the semantic content of the image at some level. A model that has truly understood “this is a fish swimming near coral” can make a reasonable prediction about what the top of the image looks like, even though it hasn’t seen it. A model that has memorized pixel statistics without understanding content cannot. This idea, seemingly simple, has produced some of the most powerful models in modern AI. The BERT family of language models is trained by masking random words and predicting them from context. The MAE (Masked Autoencoder) for images masks large random patches of an image and trains the model to reconstruct them. These self-supervised objectives, applied at scale, produce representations that transfer remarkably well to downstream tasks — often matching or exceeding the performance of supervised methods trained on large labeled datasets. The Transfer Learning Payoff What makes unsupervised and self-supervised pre-training so valuable in practice is the concept of transfer learning. The workflow proceeds in two stages: First, train the encoder (or the full self-supervised model) on a large unlabeled dataset. This pre-training phase is computationally expensive but can be done once and the result shared broadly. The model learns a rich, general-purpose intermediate representation. Second, for a specific downstream task (say, medical image classification), collect a small labeled dataset — perhaps a few thousand examples, which is far cheaper to annotate than millions. Train a lightweight classifier on top of the frozen (or lightly fine-tuned) encoder. Because the encoder has already learned to produce meaningful, compact representations, the classifier needs very little data to achieve high accuracy. This two-stage approach has become the dominant paradigm in modern AI. The large-scale pre-training provides the “representational foundation,” and the small labeled dataset provides the task-specific “finishing touches.” It is representation learning in its most practically powerful form. Conclusion: The Representation Is the Intelligence Looking across the full arc of this essay — from walking robots and Markov chains, through the hand-crafted features of classical computer vision, to learned representations and self-supervised autoencoders — a unifying theme emerges. The way you represent information is not a minor implementation detail. It is, in a deep sense, the intelligence itself. A perfect state representation that satisfies the Markov property allows simple dynamics models to make accurate predictions. A compact, disentangled intermediate representation allows a simple classifier to generalize robustly. A rich, hierarchical learned representation allows a model trained on one task to transfer to another with minimal additional data. In each case, the quality of the representation determines the ceiling on what the downstream system can achieve. The evolution from hand-crafted to learned representations is not the story of humans becoming unnecessary — it is the story of human insight being applied at a higher level of abstraction. Rather than designing features, we now design learning objectives (reconstruction loss, mask prediction, contrastive similarity), architectures (convolutional networks, transformers), and training regimes. The features emerge automatically, and they turn out to be better than what we could have designed by hand — because the data contains patterns that our intuitions don’t anticipate. The question “what is the right representation?” remains as central and difficult as ever. But we now have powerful tools for answering it empirically — by training, evaluating, visualizing, and iterating. Understanding these tools, and the conceptual framework that connects states, observations, generative models, and learned features, is the foundation for everything that follows in modern robotics and computer vision. This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 7: Representations and Representation Learning, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

entry.title: Single View Metrology
entry.content:
What a Single Photograph Knows About the World: A Deep Dive into Single View Metrology

How vanishing points, lines at infinity, and projective geometry allow us to reconstruct 3D structure — and even calibrate a camera — from a single image.

There is something quietly remarkable about the photograph you took of a city street last summer. The buildings recede into the distance, the parallel lanes of the road appear to converge at a point on the horizon, and without thinking about it, your brain instantly interprets the entire scene as three-dimensional. You know the buildings are rectangular, the road lanes are parallel, and the architecture is roughly perpendicular. But how does your brain do this from a flat, two-dimensional image? And more importantly — can a computer do the same thing, with mathematical rigor?


This is the central question of single view metrology: given only one photograph and (ideally) some knowledge of the camera that took it, how much geometric information about the 3D world can we recover? The answer, it turns out, is a surprising amount. We can deduce the orientations of planes, the directions of lines, the angles between surfaces, and even calibrate the camera itself — all without ever pointing a ruler at the real world.

To understand how this works, we need to build up a vocabulary of ideas, starting from the mathematics of transformations in 2D, moving through the elegant concept of “points at infinity,” and culminating in the powerful machinery of vanishing points and horizon lines that let us reason about 3D geometry from flat pictures.

Part 1: A Hierarchy of Transformations — What Gets Preserved and What Doesn’t

Before asking what a camera destroys when it projects the 3D world onto a 2D image, it helps to have a precise vocabulary for the kinds of transformations that exist and what each one preserves. Think of this as a ladder of increasingly permissive transformations, each rung sacrificing some geometric property in exchange for more flexibility.

Isometries: The Rigid Body

An isometric transformation is the most restrictive kind — it preserves distances. If you pick up a rigid object and move it around without bending or stretching it, you’ve performed an isometry. The object can rotate and translate, but nothing else. Mathematically, using homogeneous coordinates (where a 2D point $(x, y)$ is represented as the triple $(x, y, 1)^T$ for reasons we’ll appreciate shortly), an isometry looks like:

\[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

Here, $R$ is a $2 \times 2$ rotation matrix and $t$ is a $2 \times 1$ translation vector. Because distances are preserved, so are angles, areas, and shapes — everything you’d expect from a rigid transformation.

Similarities: Adding Scale

A similarity transformation relaxes isometries by allowing uniform scaling. A photocopy machine that enlarges or shrinks an image while keeping its shape intact is a physical analogy. The formula adds a scalar $s$ multiplied against the rotation:

\[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} sR & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad S = \begin{pmatrix} s & 0 \\ 0 & s \end{pmatrix}\]

Similarity transformations preserve shape, which means they preserve angles and ratios of lengths, even if they don’t preserve lengths themselves. Every isometry is a special similarity where $s = 1$, but not every similarity is an isometry.

Affine Transformations: Stretching and Shearing

Affine transformations are more general still. They are defined as:

\[T(\mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{t}\]

where $A$ is any invertible linear transformation. In homogeneous coordinates:

\[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

Affine transformations can scale non-uniformly, shear, and stretch — think of what happens when you view a circle painted on the ground from an oblique angle: it becomes an ellipse. Yet affine transformations still preserve a key structural property: parallelism. If two lines were parallel before the transformation, they remain parallel after it. They also preserve straight lines and ratios of distances along a line.

Projective Transformations (Homographies): The Most General Case

The final and most general transformation is the projective transformation, also called a homography. In homogeneous coordinates:

\[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ v^T & b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

The key difference from the affine case is the extra row $\begin{pmatrix} v^T & b \end{pmatrix}$ at the bottom. This seemingly small addition has a dramatic effect: projective transformations do not preserve parallelism. This is precisely what makes them the right model for what a camera does. When you photograph a tiled floor, the parallel grout lines appear to converge toward a point in the image — a projective transformation has been applied.

What does a projective transformation preserve? Two things: collinearity (points on a line remain on a line — lines map to lines) and the cross-ratio of four collinear points, defined as:

\[\text{cross ratio} = \frac{\|P_3 - P_1\| \cdot \|P_4 - P_2\|}{\|P_3 - P_2\| \cdot \|P_4 - P_1\|}\]


This cross-ratio is the deepest invariant of projective geometry — a number that doesn’t change no matter how you project or transform the four points, as long as their collinearity is maintained. It is the fingerprint that a projective transformation cannot alter.


—

Part 2: Points and Lines at Infinity — Where Parallel Lines “Meet”

Here’s a philosophical puzzle that has a beautiful mathematical resolution. Every student learns that parallel lines never intersect. And yet, when you stand on a long straight road and look toward the horizon, the road’s edges appear to converge to a single point. Which is it — do they meet or not?

The answer lies in the genius of homogeneous coordinates, which give us a unified framework to talk about both ordinary intersections and intersections “at infinity.”

Representing Lines in 2D

A line in 2D can be written as $ax + by + c = 0$, and in homogeneous form, it is represented by the vector $\ell = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \end{pmatrix}^T$. A point $\mathbf{p} = \begin{pmatrix} x & y & 1 \end{pmatrix}^T$ lies on the line if and only if $\ell^T \mathbf{p} = 0$. The ratio $-a/b$ captures the slope and $-c/b$ captures the y-intercept.

The intersection of two lines $\ell$ and $\ell’$ is elegantly given by their cross product: $\mathbf{x} = \ell \times \ell’$. You can verify this directly: by the definition of the cross product, $\mathbf{x}$ is orthogonal to both $\ell$ and $\ell’$, which in our notation means $\mathbf{x}^T \ell = 0$ and $\mathbf{x}^T \ell’ = 0$ — exactly the condition for $\mathbf{x}$ to lie on both lines.


The Beautiful Resolution: Ideal Points

Now, what happens when two lines are parallel? Their slopes are equal, meaning $a/b = a’/b’$. Computing the cross product gives:

\[\ell \times \ell' \propto \begin{pmatrix} b \\ -a \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{x}_\infty\]

Notice the last coordinate: it’s zero. In homogeneous coordinates, converting back to Euclidean coordinates requires dividing by the last coordinate. A zero last coordinate means the point is at infinity — formally, we’d be dividing by zero, which sends the point infinitely far away. This is called an ideal point or a point at infinity.

What makes this elegant is the consistency: every point of the form $(x, y, 0)^T$ in homogeneous coordinates represents a direction — a point infinitely far in that direction. And all parallel lines with slope $-a/b$ share the same ideal point $(b, -a, 0)^T$. You can verify: $\ell^T \mathbf{x}_\infty = a \cdot b + b \cdot (-a) + c \cdot 0 = 0$, so every parallel line in the family passes through that ideal point. This is the mathematical formalization of the intuition that parallel lines “meet at the horizon.”

The Line at Infinity

If we gather all the ideal points together — from every possible family of parallel lines — they all share a remarkable property: they lie on a single line at infinity, denoted $\ell_\infty$. We can define it as:

\[\ell_\infty = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^T\]

You can verify: for any ideal point $(x, y, 0)^T$, we have $\ell_\infty^T \mathbf{x}_\infty = 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + 1 \cdot 0 = 0$, so every ideal point lies on this line. The line at infinity is the mathematical home of all directions.

What Transformations Do to Points at Infinity

This is where the distinction between affine and projective transformations becomes crucially important.

Under a projective transformation $H$, a point at infinity $\mathbf{p}_\infty = (x, y, 0)^T$ gets mapped to:

\[\mathbf{p}' = H\mathbf{p}_\infty = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ v^T & b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} p'_x \\ p'_y \\ p'_z \end{pmatrix}\]

The last coordinate $p’_z = v^T (x, y)^T$ is generally nonzero, meaning the point at infinity has been mapped to an ordinary finite point. This is exactly what a camera does: it takes a direction (a point at infinity in the 3D world) and maps it to a specific pixel in the image. Parallel lines in 3D, sharing an ideal point, get mapped to lines in the image that converge at a real, observable pixel location.

Under an affine transformation, however, the bottom row is $(0, 0, 1)$, so the last coordinate of the transformed point is always $0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + 1 \cdot 0 = 0$. Affine transformations preserve the line at infinity: ideal points stay ideal, and parallelism is maintained.

Similarly, lines transform under projective transformations via $\ell’ = H^{-T} \ell$, and the line at infinity is not generally preserved by projective transformations (it gets mapped to some finite line in the image), but affine transformations do preserve it.

Part 3: Vanishing Points and Horizon Lines — The Window into 3D

We are now ready to make the leap from abstract 2D geometry into the 3D world and its relationship to images. This is where the theory becomes practically powerful.

Vanishing Points: Where the World’s Infinity Lands in Your Image

Imagine a long straight road stretching away from you. The road’s edges are parallel lines in 3D. Their ideal point — the point at infinity in the direction of the road — gets projected by the camera onto a real pixel in the image. That pixel is the vanishing point.

More precisely, suppose a family of parallel lines in 3D all run in direction $\mathbf{d} = (a, b, c)^T$ (in the camera’s coordinate frame). Their point at infinity in 3D is $(a, b, c, 0)^T$ in homogeneous 3D coordinates. The camera matrix $K$ (the intrinsic calibration matrix encoding focal length, principal point, etc.) projects this to an image point. The resulting vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ in the image satisfies:

\[\mathbf{v} = K\mathbf{d}\]


This is a strikingly simple equation. It says that the vanishing point of a family of parallel lines is completely determined by the direction of those lines and the camera’s intrinsic parameters. Conversely, if we observe a vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ in the image and know $K$, we can recover the 3D direction:

\[\mathbf{d} = \frac{K^{-1}\mathbf{v}}{\|K^{-1}\mathbf{v}\|}\]

The normalization ensures $\mathbf{d}$ is a unit vector representing a pure direction in 3D space. This is a powerful inverse operation: by looking at where lines converge in a photograph, we can recover the actual orientation of those lines in the real world.

The Horizon Line: A Plane’s Signature in the Image

A single plane in 3D (think of a tiled floor, the face of a building, or the surface of a table) contains many families of parallel lines. Each family has its own vanishing point. The horizon line (or vanishing line) of the plane is the image-line that passes through all these vanishing points.

Here’s the intuition: all families of parallel lines within a plane share the same “line at infinity” in 3D (since they all lie in the plane). When the camera projects the scene, this line at infinity in the plane maps to a specific line in the image — the horizon line. Mathematically:

\[\ell_{\text{horiz}} = H_P^{-T} \ell_\infty\]

where $H_P$ is the projective transformation induced by the camera’s projection of that particular plane.


The practical power of the horizon line is remarkable. Think about looking at a photograph of a road: even though the lane markings clearly converge in the image, you know they are parallel in the real world. The horizon line is the mathematical tool that encodes this knowledge — it tells you which line in the image corresponds to “the direction of infinity” for all lines on that road surface.

Furthermore, the horizon line encodes the orientation of the plane in 3D. If the camera is calibrated (i.e., $K$ is known), then the normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ to the plane can be extracted directly from the horizon line:

\[\mathbf{n} = K^T \ell_{\text{horiz}}\]

This is a beautiful result. The horizon line in the image — a line you can literally see and identify — encodes the perpendicular direction to the plane in 3D space. If you can find the horizon line of the floor in a photograph, you immediately know which direction is “up” relative to that floor’s surface.

Measuring Angles Between Directions and Planes

The machinery we’ve built so far allows us to do something that might seem impossible at first: measure angles between lines and planes in 3D, using only their image projections.

Suppose two families of parallel lines in 3D have directions $\mathbf{d}_1$ and $\mathbf{d}_2$, corresponding to vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ in the image. The angle $\theta$ between the directions is the angle whose cosine is $\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2 / (|\mathbf{d}_1| |\mathbf{d}_2|)$.

Substituting $\mathbf{d}_i = K^{-1}\mathbf{v}_i / |K^{-1}\mathbf{v}_i|$ and doing some algebra, this becomes:

\[\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{v}_1^T \omega \mathbf{v}_2}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_1^T \omega \mathbf{v}_1} \cdot \sqrt{\mathbf{v}_2^T \omega \mathbf{v}_2}}\]

where $\omega = (KK^T)^{-1}$. The matrix $\omega$ is called the image of the absolute conic (IAC) — it is a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix that encodes all of the camera’s intrinsic parameters in a form that is directly useful for computing angles.

Think of $\omega$ as a kind of “metric ruler” for the image plane. Ordinarily, angles in the image don’t correspond to angles in the 3D world (the camera distorts them). But $\omega$ provides the correction factor that translates image measurements back into real-world angular measurements.


Analogously, the angle between two planes in 3D can be derived from their horizon lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$:

\[\cos\theta = \frac{\ell_1^T \omega^{-1} \ell_2}{\sqrt{\ell_1^T \omega^{-1} \ell_1} \cdot \sqrt{\ell_2^T \omega^{-1} \ell_2}}\]

Both equations share the same fundamental structure: the matrix $\omega$ (or its inverse) acts as the metric that transforms the projective image coordinates into an inner product that reflects the true 3D geometry.

Part 4: Calibrating a Camera from a Single Image

Now we arrive at arguably the most remarkable application of everything we’ve developed. Normally, camera calibration requires a physical calibration target — a checkerboard pattern photographed from many angles, for instance. But what if we already have a single photograph of a structured scene, with no calibration target in sight? Can we recover the camera’s intrinsic parameters $K$ from the photograph alone?

The answer is yes, under certain conditions.

The Setup: Orthogonal Planes in the Scene

The key observation is that the constraint “$\cos\theta = 0$” (i.e., two lines or planes are perpendicular) is one of the most common geometric constraints we encounter in man-made environments. Buildings have walls that meet at right angles, rooms have floors and ceilings that are perpendicular to walls, and corridors contain edges that are mutually orthogonal. We can exploit this structure.

Suppose we identify two families of parallel lines in the image — one for each of two planes that we know (from context) are perpendicular in 3D. We extract the two vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$. Since the corresponding directions are perpendicular ($\theta = 90°$, so $\cos\theta = 0$), the formula above gives:

\[\mathbf{v}_1^T \omega \mathbf{v}_2 = 0\]

This is one equation in the unknown $\omega$. How many unknowns does $\omega$ have? Since $\omega = (KK^T)^{-1}$ and $K$ has 5 degrees of freedom (in general: focal length, aspect ratio, skew, and two principal point coordinates), $\omega$ is a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix with at most 6 independent entries. Since $\omega$ is only known up to scale (an overall scaling factor doesn’t affect the angle formulas), we effectively have 5 unknowns.


One pair of perpendicular vanishing points gives 1 constraint. Two pairs give 2 constraints. Three mutually perpendicular pairs — which correspond to three orthogonal planes, like the three faces of a room corner — give 3 constraints:

\[\mathbf{v}_1^T \omega \mathbf{v}_2 = 0, \quad \mathbf{v}_1^T \omega \mathbf{v}_3 = 0, \quad \mathbf{v}_2^T \omega \mathbf{v}_3 = 0\]

That’s still only 3 constraints for 5 unknowns. We’re short by 2. Here is where a common and practically reasonable assumption saves us: if we assume the camera has zero skew (the pixels are rectangular, not parallelogram-shaped) and square pixels (equal horizontal and vertical pixel density), then $\omega$ takes the simplified form:

\[\omega = \begin{pmatrix} \omega_1 & 0 & \omega_4 \\ 0 & \omega_1 & \omega_5 \\ \omega_4 & \omega_5 & \omega_6 \end{pmatrix}\]

This form has only 4 distinct parameters. Since $\omega$ is determined only up to scale, we effectively have 3 free parameters. The three orthogonality constraints from three mutually perpendicular vanishing points are exactly enough to solve for this $\omega$.

From $\omega$ to $K$: Cholesky Decomposition

Once $\omega$ is determined, recovering $K$ is a standard numerical procedure. Recall that $\omega = (KK^T)^{-1}$, which means $\omega^{-1} = KK^T$. This says that $\omega^{-1}$ is a positive-definite symmetric matrix with a specific factorization. The Cholesky decomposition finds the unique lower-triangular matrix $L$ such that $\omega^{-1} = LL^T$. Since $K$ must be upper-triangular (by convention in camera models), we identify $K = L^T$.

The entire pipeline thus looks like this: identify three mutually perpendicular planes in the image → find their vanishing points → set up the three orthogonality equations → solve for $\omega$ → apply Cholesky decomposition → obtain $K$. A single photograph, with no calibration target, has yielded the full intrinsic calibration of the camera.


What Comes Next: Recovering 3D Geometry

With $K$ in hand, the door to 3D reconstruction swings open. For any plane visible in the image, we can:

  • Find the horizon line of that plane (from the vanishing points of lines in the plane).
  • Recover the plane’s 3D normal direction via $\mathbf{n} = K^T \ell_{\text{horiz}}$.
  • Compute angles between planes using their horizon lines and $\omega^{-1}$.
  • Recover the 3D directions of any family of parallel lines using $\mathbf{d} = K^{-1}\mathbf{v} / |K^{-1}\mathbf{v}|$.

What began as a flat photograph has been transformed, through the mathematics of projective geometry, into a partial but rich 3D model of the scene.

Part 5: Conceptual Synthesis — What the Mathematics Tells Us

It is worth pausing to appreciate the conceptual arc of what we have covered.


The projective transformation is the right mathematical model for what a camera does. It destroys some geometric information — most notably, parallelism — but it preserves other things: the cross-ratio of four collinear points, collinearity itself, and crucially, the directions of parallel lines (in the form of vanishing points). The camera does not destroy information randomly; it transforms it in a systematic, invertible (given enough constraints) way.

The line at infinity in 2D, and the plane at infinity in 3D, are not mystical constructs but practical tools. The plane at infinity in 3D — defined by the vector $(0, 0, 0, 1)^T$ in homogeneous coordinates — is the “home” of all directions in 3D space. When the camera projects the scene, it maps this plane at infinity to a finite region of the image, and the structure of that mapping (encoded by $\omega$) tells us everything about how the camera distorts angles. Recovering $\omega$ is equivalent to understanding how the camera has “compressed” the plane at infinity into the image.

The assumption of zero skew and square pixels is worth reflecting on. These are not exotic constraints — they are satisfied by virtually every modern digital camera. By incorporating this common-sense knowledge about camera construction, we close the gap between the geometric constraints available from the scene and the number of unknowns in the camera model. Prior knowledge about the camera compensates for what the scene cannot tell us alone.

There is also a beautiful symmetry in the angle formulas. The same matrix $\omega = (KK^T)^{-1}$ appears in both the line-direction angle formula and the plane-normal angle formula (using $\omega^{-1}$ in the latter). This is not a coincidence: $\omega$ is precisely the metric tensor of the image plane that corrects for the projective distortion of the camera. It is the Rosetta Stone that translates between image measurements and 3D angular measurements.

Conclusion: One Image, a World of Information

The ideas explored here collectively answer a question that might initially seem impossible: what can one photograph tell us about the 3D world that produced it? As we have seen, the answer is “quite a lot” — provided we know how to listen.

The hierarchy of transformations — from rigid isometries to similarities, affinities, and finally projective transformations — establishes the precise way in which perspective imaging distorts the world. The concept of points and lines at infinity provides a mathematically coherent way to talk about direction and parallelism even in the projected image. Vanishing points are the image of these ideal points, and they encode the 3D directions of parallel lines. Horizon lines encode the orientation of planes. And the matrix $\omega$, derived from the camera’s intrinsic parameters, is the key that unlocks angular measurements from image coordinates alone.

The culminating result — that three mutually perpendicular vanishing points from a single photograph, combined with the mild assumption of a well-behaved camera, are sufficient to calibrate the camera — is a testament to how much structure is hidden inside an ordinary image. Every photograph of an architectural scene, a room interior, or a city street is simultaneously a record of the visual scene and a rich geometric document waiting to be decoded.

This is the spirit of single view metrology: not merely asking what a photograph shows, but asking what the geometry of the photograph reveals about the world that made it.

This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 2: Single View Metrology, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.
entry.summary: What a Single Photograph Knows About the World: A Deep Dive into Single View Metrology How vanishing points, lines at infinity, and projective geometry allow us to reconstruct 3D structure — and even calibrate a camera — from a single image. There is something quietly remarkable about the photograph you took of a city street last summer. The buildings recede into the distance, the parallel lanes of the road appear to converge at a point on the horizon, and without thinking about it, your brain instantly interprets the entire scene as three-dimensional. You know the buildings are rectangular, the road lanes are parallel, and the architecture is roughly perpendicular. But how does your brain do this from a flat, two-dimensional image? And more importantly — can a computer do the same thing, with mathematical rigor? This is the central question of single view metrology: given only one photograph and (ideally) some knowledge of the camera that took it, how much geometric information about the 3D world can we recover? The answer, it turns out, is a surprising amount. We can deduce the orientations of planes, the directions of lines, the angles between surfaces, and even calibrate the camera itself — all without ever pointing a ruler at the real world. To understand how this works, we need to build up a vocabulary of ideas, starting from the mathematics of transformations in 2D, moving through the elegant concept of “points at infinity,” and culminating in the powerful machinery of vanishing points and horizon lines that let us reason about 3D geometry from flat pictures. Part 1: A Hierarchy of Transformations — What Gets Preserved and What Doesn’t Before asking what a camera destroys when it projects the 3D world onto a 2D image, it helps to have a precise vocabulary for the kinds of transformations that exist and what each one preserves. Think of this as a ladder of increasingly permissive transformations, each rung sacrificing some geometric property in exchange for more flexibility. Isometries: The Rigid Body An isometric transformation is the most restrictive kind — it preserves distances. If you pick up a rigid object and move it around without bending or stretching it, you’ve performed an isometry. The object can rotate and translate, but nothing else. Mathematically, using homogeneous coordinates (where a 2D point $(x, y)$ is represented as the triple $(x, y, 1)^T$ for reasons we’ll appreciate shortly), an isometry looks like: \[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\] Here, $R$ is a $2 \times 2$ rotation matrix and $t$ is a $2 \times 1$ translation vector. Because distances are preserved, so are angles, areas, and shapes — everything you’d expect from a rigid transformation. Similarities: Adding Scale A similarity transformation relaxes isometries by allowing uniform scaling. A photocopy machine that enlarges or shrinks an image while keeping its shape intact is a physical analogy. The formula adds a scalar $s$ multiplied against the rotation: \[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} sR & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad S=\begin{pmatrix} s & 0 \\ 0 & s \end{pmatrix}\] Similarity transformations preserve shape, which means they preserve angles and ratios of lengths, even if they don’t preserve lengths themselves. Every isometry is a special similarity where $s = 1$, but not every similarity is an isometry. Affine Transformations: Stretching and Shearing Affine transformations are more general still. They are defined as: \[T(\mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{t}\] where $A$ is any invertible linear transformation. In homogeneous coordinates: \[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\] Affine transformations can scale non-uniformly, shear, and stretch — think of what happens when you view a circle painted on the ground from an oblique angle: it becomes an ellipse. Yet affine transformations still preserve a key structural property: parallelism. If two lines were parallel before the transformation, they remain parallel after it. They also preserve straight lines and ratios of distances along a line. Projective Transformations (Homographies): The Most General Case The final and most general transformation is the projective transformation, also called a homography. In homogeneous coordinates: \[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ v^T & b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\] The key difference from the affine case is the extra row $\begin{pmatrix} v^T & b \end{pmatrix}$ at the bottom. This seemingly small addition has a dramatic effect: projective transformations do not preserve parallelism. This is precisely what makes them the right model for what a camera does. When you photograph a tiled floor, the parallel grout lines appear to converge toward a point in the image — a projective transformation has been applied. What does a projective transformation preserve? Two things: collinearity (points on a line remain on a line — lines map to lines) and the cross-ratio of four collinear points, defined as: \[\text{cross ratio} = \frac{\|P_3 - P_1\| \cdot \|P_4 - P_2\|}{\|P_3 - P_2\| \cdot \|P_4 - P_1\|}\] This cross-ratio is the deepest invariant of projective geometry — a number that doesn’t change no matter how you project or transform the four points, as long as their collinearity is maintained. It is the fingerprint that a projective transformation cannot alter. — Part 2: Points and Lines at Infinity — Where Parallel Lines “Meet” Here’s a philosophical puzzle that has a beautiful mathematical resolution. Every student learns that parallel lines never intersect. And yet, when you stand on a long straight road and look toward the horizon, the road’s edges appear to converge to a single point. Which is it — do they meet or not? The answer lies in the genius of homogeneous coordinates, which give us a unified framework to talk about both ordinary intersections and intersections “at infinity.” Representing Lines in 2D A line in 2D can be written as $ax + by + c=0$, and in homogeneous form, it is represented by the vector $\ell = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \end{pmatrix}^T$. A point $\mathbf{p} = \begin{pmatrix} x & y & 1 \end{pmatrix}^T$ lies on the line if and only if $\ell^T \mathbf{p} = 0$. The ratio $-a/b$ captures the slope and $-c/b$ captures the y-intercept. The intersection of two lines $\ell$ and $\ell’$ is elegantly given by their cross product: $\mathbf{x} = \ell \times \ell’$. You can verify this directly: by the definition of the cross product, $\mathbf{x}$ is orthogonal to both $\ell$ and $\ell’$, which in our notation means $\mathbf{x}^T \ell = 0$ and $\mathbf{x}^T \ell’ = 0$ — exactly the condition for $\mathbf{x}$ to lie on both lines. The Beautiful Resolution: Ideal Points Now, what happens when two lines are parallel? Their slopes are equal, meaning $a/b = a’/b’$. Computing the cross product gives: \[\ell \times \ell' \propto \begin{pmatrix} b \\ -a \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{x}_\infty\] Notice the last coordinate: it’s zero. In homogeneous coordinates, converting back to Euclidean coordinates requires dividing by the last coordinate. A zero last coordinate means the point is at infinity — formally, we’d be dividing by zero, which sends the point infinitely far away. This is called an ideal point or a point at infinity. What makes this elegant is the consistency: every point of the form $(x, y, 0)^T$ in homogeneous coordinates represents a direction — a point infinitely far in that direction. And all parallel lines with slope $-a/b$ share the same ideal point $(b, -a, 0)^T$. You can verify: $\ell^T \mathbf{x}_\infty = a \cdot b + b \cdot (-a) + c \cdot 0=0$, so every parallel line in the family passes through that ideal point. This is the mathematical formalization of the intuition that parallel lines “meet at the horizon.” The Line at Infinity If we gather all the ideal points together — from every possible family of parallel lines — they all share a remarkable property: they lie on a single line at infinity, denoted $\ell_\infty$. We can define it as: \[\ell_\infty = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^T\] You can verify: for any ideal point $(x, y, 0)^T$, we have $\ell_\infty^T \mathbf{x}_\infty = 0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + 1 \cdot 0=0$, so every ideal point lies on this line. The line at infinity is the mathematical home of all directions. What Transformations Do to Points at Infinity This is where the distinction between affine and projective transformations becomes crucially important. Under a projective transformation $H$, a point at infinity $\mathbf{p}_\infty = (x, y, 0)^T$ gets mapped to: \[\mathbf{p}' = H\mathbf{p}_\infty = \begin{pmatrix} A & t \\ v^T & b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} p'_x \\ p'_y \\ p'_z \end{pmatrix}\] The last coordinate $p’_z = v^T (x, y)^T$ is generally nonzero, meaning the point at infinity has been mapped to an ordinary finite point. This is exactly what a camera does: it takes a direction (a point at infinity in the 3D world) and maps it to a specific pixel in the image. Parallel lines in 3D, sharing an ideal point, get mapped to lines in the image that converge at a real, observable pixel location. Under an affine transformation, however, the bottom row is $(0, 0, 1)$, so the last coordinate of the transformed point is always $0 \cdot x + 0 \cdot y + 1 \cdot 0=0$. Affine transformations preserve the line at infinity: ideal points stay ideal, and parallelism is maintained. Similarly, lines transform under projective transformations via $\ell’ = H^{-T} \ell$, and the line at infinity is not generally preserved by projective transformations (it gets mapped to some finite line in the image), but affine transformations do preserve it. Part 3: Vanishing Points and Horizon Lines — The Window into 3D We are now ready to make the leap from abstract 2D geometry into the 3D world and its relationship to images. This is where the theory becomes practically powerful. Vanishing Points: Where the World’s Infinity Lands in Your Image Imagine a long straight road stretching away from you. The road’s edges are parallel lines in 3D. Their ideal point — the point at infinity in the direction of the road — gets projected by the camera onto a real pixel in the image. That pixel is the vanishing point. More precisely, suppose a family of parallel lines in 3D all run in direction $\mathbf{d} = (a, b, c)^T$ (in the camera’s coordinate frame). Their point at infinity in 3D is $(a, b, c, 0)^T$ in homogeneous 3D coordinates. The camera matrix $K$ (the intrinsic calibration matrix encoding focal length, principal point, etc.) projects this to an image point. The resulting vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ in the image satisfies: \[\mathbf{v} = K\mathbf{d}\] This is a strikingly simple equation. It says that the vanishing point of a family of parallel lines is completely determined by the direction of those lines and the camera’s intrinsic parameters. Conversely, if we observe a vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ in the image and know $K$, we can recover the 3D direction: \[\mathbf{d} = \frac{K^{-1}\mathbf{v}}{\|K^{-1}\mathbf{v}\|}\] The normalization ensures $\mathbf{d}$ is a unit vector representing a pure direction in 3D space. This is a powerful inverse operation: by looking at where lines converge in a photograph, we can recover the actual orientation of those lines in the real world. If you can find the horizon line of the floor in a photograph, you immediately know which direction is “up” relative to that floor’s surface. The plane at infinity in 3D — defined by the vector $(0, 0, 0, 1)^T$ in homogeneous coordinates — is the “home” of all directions in 3D space. When the camera projects the scene, it maps this plane at infinity to a finite region of the image, and the structure of that mapping (encoded by $\omega$) tells us everything about how the camera distorts angles. Recovering $\omega$ is equivalent to understanding how the camera has “compressed” the plane at infinity into the image. The assumption of zero skew and square pixels is worth reflecting on. These are not exotic constraints — they are satisfied by virtually every modern digital camera. By incorporating this common-sense knowledge about camera construction, we close the gap between the geometric constraints available from the scene and the number of unknowns in the camera model. Prior knowledge about the camera compensates for what the scene cannot tell us alone. There is also a beautiful symmetry in the angle formulas. The same matrix $\omega = (KK^T)^{-1}$ appears in both the line-direction angle formula and the plane-normal angle formula (using $\omega^{-1}$ in the latter). This is not a coincidence: $\omega$ is precisely the metric tensor of the image plane that corrects for the projective distortion of the camera. It is the Rosetta Stone that translates between image measurements and 3D angular measurements. Conclusion: One Image, a World of Information The ideas explored here collectively answer a question that might initially seem impossible: what can one photograph tell us about the 3D world that produced it? As we have seen, the answer is “quite a lot” — provided we know how to listen. The hierarchy of transformations — from rigid isometries to similarities, affinities, and finally projective transformations — establishes the precise way in which perspective imaging distorts the world. The concept of points and lines at infinity provides a mathematically coherent way to talk about direction and parallelism even in the projected image. Vanishing points are the image of these ideal points, and they encode the 3D directions of parallel lines. Horizon lines encode the orientation of planes. And the matrix $\omega$, derived from the camera’s intrinsic parameters, is the key that unlocks angular measurements from image coordinates alone. The culminating result — that three mutually perpendicular vanishing points from a single photograph, combined with the mild assumption of a well-behaved camera, are sufficient to calibrate the camera — is a testament to how much structure is hidden inside an ordinary image. Every photograph of an architectural scene, a room interior, or a city street is simultaneously a record of the visual scene and a rich geometric document waiting to be decoded. This is the spirit of single view metrology: not merely asking what a photograph shows, but asking what the geometry of the photograph reveals about the world that made it. This article is based on CS231A Course Notes 2: Single View Metrology, by Kenji Hata and Silvio Savarese, Stanford University.

entry.title: Stereo Systems
entry.content:
Seeing in 3D: How Computers Reconstruct the World from Flat Images

A deep dive into triangulation, stereo vision, and structure from motion — the algorithms that let machines perceive depth.

Introduction: The Depth Illusion

Close one eye and reach for a nearby object. You will likely miss it — or at least feel strangely uncertain about how far away it is. Your visual system suddenly loses something it normally takes for granted: depth. The brain reconstructs a 3D world by comparing the slightly different images received by each eye, a process called stereopsis. The difference in position of an object between the two eyes — called disparity — encodes how far away the object is.


Cameras, unlike eyes, capture flat 2D images. A single photograph flattens the entire richness of a three-dimensional scene into a plane, discarding depth information entirely. A point appearing in a photograph could be close and small, or far away and large — the image alone cannot tell you which. This is the fundamental challenge of 3D computer vision: recovering the depth, structure, and geometry of a world that has been projected down onto a flat sensor.

Yet this is exactly what modern systems do, with remarkable success. The GPS in your phone reconstructs satellite geometry to locate you on Earth. Autonomous vehicles build 3D maps in real time from cameras. Photogrammetry software turns a handful of vacation photos into a detailed 3D model of a cathedral. Augmented reality apps overlay digital objects onto the physical world with precise spatial alignment. All of these depend on the same core algorithmic ideas: triangulation, stereo reconstruction, and structure from motion (SfM).

In this article, we will build up these ideas from first principles — not just explaining what the algorithms do, but why they work, what makes them tricky in practice, and how the mathematics captures the geometry of vision.

Part 1: Triangulation — Finding Where Rays Meet

The Core Idea

Here is the simplest version of the 3D reconstruction problem. You have two cameras, both looking at the same scene. You can see the same physical point $P$ in both images — at position $p$ in the first image and $p’$ in the second. You know everything about both cameras: their intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point, pixel scaling) encoded in matrices $K$ and $K’$, and their relative rotation $R$ and translation $T$ with respect to each other.


Given all of this, where is $P$ in 3D space?

The answer seems almost obvious once you draw the picture. Each observed image point, combined with the camera center, defines a ray in 3D space — a line emanating from the camera through the image point and extending into the scene. The first camera gives you ray $\ell$, the second gives you ray $\ell’$. The 3D point $P$ must lie on both rays simultaneously, so $P$ is simply the intersection of $\ell$ and $\ell’$. This is the essence of triangulation.

Think of it like two search parties trying to locate a missing hiker from different mountain peaks. Each party can see the hiker’s fire and knows what direction it lies in — but not the distance. If both parties know exactly where they are standing and which direction they are looking, they can draw two lines on a map and find where the lines cross. That crossing point is where the fire must be.

Why Perfect Intersection Rarely Exists

In theory, the two rays $\ell$ and $\ell’$ must intersect — after all, they both pass through the same physical point $P$. In practice, they almost never intersect cleanly.

The culprit is noise. The pixel locations $p$ and $p’$ are measured with some error due to sensor noise, lens distortion, and quantization effects. The camera calibration parameters $K$, $K’$, $R$, $T$ are also estimated from data, and thus carry their own errors. When you compute the rays based on imprecise inputs, the rays end up slightly skewed — passing near each other but not through a common point. In 3D space, two lines that are not parallel and do not intersect are called skew lines, and skew lines are the rule rather than the exception in real-world triangulation.


This means we cannot simply find an exact intersection. Instead, we need to find the best approximate answer. There are two main strategies for doing this, each with different trade-offs.

Strategy 1: The Linear Method (DLT)

The first approach reformulates triangulation as a system of linear equations. Starting from the projection equation $p = MP$ (where $M$ is the $3 \times 4$ camera matrix), we use a key algebraic observation: since $p$ and $MP$ represent the same point in homogeneous coordinates, their cross product is zero:

\[p \times (MP) = 0\]

Expanding this cross product gives three scalar equations:

\(x(M_3 P) - (M_1 P) = 0\) \(y(M_3 P) - (M_2 P) = 0\) \(x(M_2 P) - y(M_1 P) = 0\)

where $M_i$ denotes the $i$-th row of the camera matrix $M$, and $(x, y, 1)$ are the homogeneous coordinates of the image point $p$. Each observed correspondence contributes a pair of independent constraints (the third equation is redundant). Stacking the constraints from both cameras, we get a homogeneous linear system:

\[A P = 0, \quad \text{where} \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} xM_3 - M_1 \\ yM_3 - M_2 \\ x'M'_3 - M'_1 \\ y'M'_3 - M'_2 \end{pmatrix}\]

This is a standard Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) problem. We find the vector $P$ that minimizes $|AP|$ subject to $|P| = 1$, which is simply the right singular vector of $A$ corresponding to its smallest singular value.

One elegant property of this formulation is that it generalizes seamlessly to more than two cameras. If you add a third camera with its own observation, you simply append two more rows to the matrix $A$. The SVD solution naturally incorporates all available observations.

However, the linear method has a critical flaw: it is not invariant under projective transformations. If we apply a projective transformation $H$ to the camera matrices (replacing $M$ with $MH^{-1}$), the system matrix becomes $AH^{-1}$, and the old solution $P$ now corresponds to $HP$ in the new coordinate system. But the SVD imposes the constraint $|P| = 1$, which is not preserved under a projective transformation $H$. This means that in projective reconstruction settings, the linear method does not give the geometrically optimal answer. It is a convenient starting point, but not the final word.

Strategy 2: The Nonlinear Method (Minimizing Reprojection Error)

A more principled approach frames triangulation as a minimization problem. Rather than asking “where do the rays intersect?” we ask: “what 3D point, when projected into both cameras, best explains the observed image points?”

Formally, we want to find a 3D point $\hat{P}$ that minimizes the total reprojection error:

\[\min_{\hat{P}} \; \|M\hat{P} - p\|^2 + \|M'\hat{P} - p'\|^2\]

The term $|M\hat{P} - p|^2$ measures the pixel distance between where $\hat{P}$ actually projects in image 1 (at $M\hat{P}$) and where we observed it (at $p$). This is the reprojection error for image 1. The full objective sums these errors across all images:

\[\min_{\hat{P}} \; \sum_i \|M_i \hat{P} - p_i\|^2\]
